VIP signaling abnormalities may lead to circadian desynchronization. [ 140 , 141 ] 3. Molecular pathways linking circadian clock genes to insomnia 3.1. Gene expression variations and neurotransmitter regulation The circadian clock command center of mammals is located in the SCN of the hypothalamus. At the molecular level, the SCN receives and integrates light signals to drive the transcription and translation of clock genes, forming a self-regulating transcription–translation feedback loop (TTFL) [ 39 ]. The core loop of TTFL consists of CLOCK, BMAL1, PER, and CRY genes. In the early morning, CLOCK and BMAL1 form a heterodimer CLOCK/BMAL1, bind to the E-box element in the promoter region of target genes, and activate the transcription of PER1-3 and CRY1-2 [ 40 ]. In the evening, after PER proteins are phosphorylated by casein kinase 1 (CK1), they form a CK1/PER/CRY complex with CRY proteins, which in turn inhibits the transcriptional activity of CLOCK/BMAL1, creating a negative feedback mechanism [ 41 ]. In addition, other regulatory loops, such as NR1D1/REV–Erbα, RORα, and Differentially Expressed in Chondrocytes 1/2 (DEC1-2), also fine-tune the main loop to ensure molecular circadian rhythmicity and form a nearly 24-hour circadian cycle [ 42 ]. The SCN regulates sleep rhythms through neural projections and neurotransmitter diffusion. During wakefulness, the SCN projects to arousal-promoting nuclei such as the locus coeruleus (LC), dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN), and tuberomammillary nucleus (TMN)  via  the ventral subparaventricular zone (vSPZ) and dorsomedial hypothalamus (DMH), while inhibiting the sleep-promoting ventral lateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) [ 43 ]. During sleep, the VLPO inhibits the LC, DRN, and TMN, and SCN neurons project to the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) to regulate melatonin (MT) synthesis [ 44 ]. Borbély’s ‘two-process model’ further explains circadian sleep regulation. It proposes that sleep is regulated by two interacting processes: the homeostatic sleep drive (process S) and the circadian pacemaker (process C) [ 45 ]. As wake time increases, process S promotes deep sleep in the early night. In the late night, process S declines and process C dominates, promoting arousal. Research shows that clock gene expression in insomniacs differs significantly. For instance, Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) patients show rhythmic loss of PER2 and BMAL1 expression in oral mucosa. Some insomniacs carry CLOCK gene polymorphisms like rs1801260 T/C, linked to ADHD-related insomnia [ 46 , 47 ]. Additionally, Per2Brdm1 mutant mice exhibit reduced glutamate transporter Eaat1 mRNA and protein levels. This causes decreased glial glutamate uptake and increased extracellular glutamate, possibly explaining alcohol-related insomnia mechanisms [ 48 ]. The interaction between circadian clocks and neurotransmitter systems is crucial for sleep regulation. Melatonin secretion, controlled strictly by the SCN, rises at night to promote sleep [ 49 ]. The light–dark cycle synchronizes the circadian clock by regulating Per gene expression in the SCN, which in turn affects melatonin rhythm [ 50 ]. Melatonin also provides feedback to regulate the circadian clock by binding to Melatonin Receptor 1/2 (MT1/2) in the SCN, inducing Per1 and Per2 expression, or by inhibiting glutamate activity to stabilize circadian rhythm [ 51 ]. Similarly, 5-Hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) system is influenced by the circadian clock, with its synthesis and secretion following a circadian rhythm likely regulated indirectly by the SCN [ 52 ]. 5-HT modulates SCN activity through its receptors (e.g. 5-HT1B, 5-HT7, 5-HT2C) and reuptake transporters, thereby affecting circadian rhythm. SSRIs can adjust circadian rhythms by altering clock gene expression in the SCN [ 52 , 53 ]. Abnormalities in circadian clock gene expression and neurotransmitter dysfunction can create a vicious cycle that exacerbates insomnia. For example, dopamine transport and degradation-related gene expression in clock gene-mutated mice shows circadian disorganization, potentially affecting reward-motivated behavior, and dopamine system abnormalities are linked to insomnia [ 54 ]. Moreover, neurotransmitter level changes may further disrupt clock gene expression, destabilize rhythms, and worsen sleep disorders [ 55 , 56 ]. 3.2. Cellular and molecular pathways leading to insomnia There are complex interactions between circadian clock genes and cellular pathways, and these interactions jointly contribute to the development of insomnia. These pathways encompass metabolic regulation, inflammatory signaling, mitochondrial dysfunction, and epigenetic modifications, all of which intersect with circadian rhythms to disrupt sleep homeostasis. 3.2.1. Metabolic dysregulation and energy homeostasis Circadian clock genes, particularly BMAL1 and CLOCK, govern metabolic processes by regulating genes involved in glucose metabolism, lipid synthesis, and mitochondrial function [ 19 ]. Disruption of these genes impairs cellular energy balance, which is critical for maintaining sleep–wake cycles. For instance, Bmal1 knockout mice exhibit hypoglycemia and altered Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) production in the hypothalamus, leading to fragmented sleep and reduced non-REM sleep duration [ 57 ]. Similarly, Clock mutant models show dysregulated hepatic lipid metabolism, which correlates with increased nighttime activity and sleep fragmentation [ 13 ]. These metabolic disturbances may impair the SCN signaling, thereby destabilizing circadian output to sleep-regulatory brain regions [ 44 , 58 ]. Thus, metabolic dysregulation caused by circadian clock gene disruptions directly contributes to insomnia by compromising the energy-dependent processes necessary for stable sleep initiation and maintenance. 3.2.2. Inflammatory signaling and neuroimmune crosstalk Chronic low-grade inflammation is increasingly recognized as a contributor to insomnia. Circadian clock genes modulate immune responses by regulating the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-α [ 59 ]. For example, PER2 deficiency in mice elevates systemic IL-6 levels, which disrupts SCN neuronal activity and promotes hyperarousal states characteristic of insomnia [ 60 ]. In humans, polymorphisms in CRY1 are associated with elevated inflammatory markers and increased insomnia severity, suggesting a bidirectional relationship between circadian dysfunction and neuroinflammation [ 61 ]. Furthermore, microglial activation in sleep-regulatory regions, driven by circadian misalignment, may exacerbate synaptic pruning abnormalities and sleep continuity issues [ 62 ]. Therefore, neuroinflammatory processes stemming from circadian disruption play a direct role in insomnia pathogenesis by inducing hyperarousal and impairing sleep-regulatory neural circuits. 3.2.3. Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress Mitochondrial rhythms, synchronized by circadian clock genes, are essential for maintaining redox balance. REV–ERBα, a key circadian nuclear receptor, regulates mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative phosphorylation [ 21 ]. Knockdown of REV–ERBα in mice increases reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in the SCN, impairing neuronal firing and melatonin secretion [ 63 ]. Beyond their damaging effects at high levels, ROS also act as signaling molecules that modulate various cellular processes, including inflammatory responses and neuronal excitability, which are implicated in sleep regulation [ 64 ]. Elevated ROS levels also inhibit BMAL1 transcription, creating a vicious cycle that exacerbates circadian disruption and sleep fragmentation [ 65 ]. This dual role of ROS—as both damaging agents and signaling molecules—further links mitochondrial dysfunction to the pathophysiology of insomnia. Clinical studies report elevated oxidative stress markers in insomniacs, correlating with reduced slow-wave sleep and impaired cognitive function [ 66 ]. Consequently, mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress directly contribute to insomnia by disrupting neuronal energy metabolism and promoting cellular damage in sleep-regulatory regions. 3.2.4. Epigenetic modifications and circadian plasticity Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation and histone acetylation, dynamically regulate circadian gene expression. For example, hypermethylation of the CLOCK promoter reduces its transcriptional activity, leading to delayed sleep phase phenotypes [ 67 ]. Additionally, specific histone marks such as H3K27ac (associated with active enhancers) and H3K4me3 (linked to active promoters) show circadian oscillations in the SCN and are altered in animal models of sleep disruption [ 68 ]. Reduced H3K27ac levels at the Per2 promoter, for instance, have been correlated with impaired sleep homeostasis [ 67 ]. Histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors, such as valproic acid, rescue Per2 expression in animal models of shift work disorder, restoring sleep architecture [ 68 ]. Furthermore, the histone methyltransferase MLL1, which catalyzes H3K4me3, is regulated by CLOCK:BMAL1 and influences circadian period length [ 69 ]. SIRT1, an NAD+-dependent deacetylase, also contributes to circadian regulation by modulating CLOCK activity and PER2 stability [ 70 ]. Additionally, circadian lncRNAs (e.g. Per2AS) interact with chromatin modifiers to fine-tune rhythmic gene expression, offering novel targets for insomnia therapy [ 71 ]. These epigenetic alterations directly link circadian clock dysfunction to insomnia by stably modifying gene expression patterns that regulate sleep–wake cycles, thereby perpetuating sleep disturbances even in the absence of initial triggers. 3.2.5. Synaptic plasticity and neuronal excitability Circadian clocks regulate synaptic strength and neurotransmitter receptor trafficking. BMAL1 modulates glutamatergic signaling by controlling the expression of NMDA receptor subunits in the prefrontal cortex, a region critical for sleep initiation [ 72 ]. Mice lacking Bmal1 exhibit hyperexcitability in cortical neurons, mirroring the hyperarousal observed in insomnia [ 73 ]. Similarly, CRY1 regulates GABAergic neurotransmission in the thalamus, and its mutation reduces sleep spindle density, impairing sleep maintenance [ 74 ]. These findings underscore the role of clock genes in maintaining synaptic equilibrium necessary for stable sleep. These findings underscore the role of clock genes in maintaining synaptic equilibrium necessary for stable sleep, and their dysfunction directly promotes insomnia by increasing neuronal excitability and disrupting inhibitory balance. In summary, insomnia arises from a confluence of cellular and molecular disruptions rooted in circadian clock dysfunction. Targeting these pathways—through metabolic interventions, anti-inflammatory agents, antioxidants, or epigenetic modulators—holds promise for developing precision therapies ( Figure 1 ). Figure 1. Molecular pathways linking circadian clock dysfunction to insomnia. Genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors disrupt the core circadian feedback loop, leading to neurotransmitter dysregulation, metabolic imbalance, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and epigenetic alterations, which collectively contribute to insomnia. 4. Circadian clock gene targeted therapy 4.1. Melatonin receptor agonists Melatonin receptor agonists (MRAs) are a first-line circadian-aligned therapy for insomnia, leveraging melatonin’s role in synchronizing the SCN and peripheral clocks. By binding to MT1 and MT2 receptors, MRAs replicate endogenous melatonin’s dual effects: MT1 activation inhibits SCN neuronal firing to promote sleep initiation, while MT2 regulates phase shifts to stabilize circadian alignment [ 75 , 76 ]. Ramelteon, a selective MT1/MT2 agonist, reduces sleep latency by 10–15 min in chronic insomnia patients, particularly those with delayed sleep phase disorder (DSPD) [ 77 ]. A randomized controlled trial involving 829 adults demonstrated that ramelteon improved sleep efficiency by 8% compared to placebo, with effects persisting over 6 months [ 78 ]. Mechanistically, ramelteon enhances PER2 and CRY1 expression in the SCN, reinforcing disrupted feedback loops in circadian misalignment [ 79 ]. However, its efficacy diminishes in shift workers with inconsistent light exposure, highlighting the need for adjunct light therapy [ 80 ]. Agomelatine, a dual MT1/MT2 agonist and 5-HT2C antagonist, addresses both circadian misalignment and comorbid depression. A 12-week trial in 332 patients with depression-related insomnia reported a 30% reduction in nighttime awakenings and a 20% increase in slow-wave sleep (SWS) duration, likely  via  PER1 upregulation in the prefrontal cortex [ 81 ]. Agomelatine’s 5-HT2C blockade further reduces hyperarousal, making it suitable for insomnia with mood disorders. However, its use is limited by hepatotoxicity risks, requiring regular liver function monitoring [ 82 ]. For non-4-hour sleep–wake disorder (N24SWD) in blind individuals, tasimelteon demonstrates unique efficacy [ 83 ]. In phase III trials, tasimelteon normalized circadian phase in 68% of participants by upregulating BMAL1 and PER1 expression, reducing sleep fragmentation by 40% over 6 months [ 84 ]. Preclinical studies in rodents reveal tasimelteon’s neuroprotective effects, reducing hippocampal oxidative stress markers (e.g. malondialdehyde) by 50% through MT2-mediated activation of the Nrf2 pathway [ 85 ]. Despite these advantages, MRAs face limitations. Approximately 15–20% of users report transient dizziness or daytime fatigue, likely due to off-target receptor interactions [ 86 ]. Efficacy is also subtype-dependent; MRAs show minimal benefit in primary insomnia unrelated to circadian disruption [ 87 ]. Long-term safety data (>1 year) remain sparse, necessitating further studies on receptor desensitization and tolerance. In clinical practice, MRAs are most effective when combined with behavioral interventions (e.g. timed light exposure) and tailored to circadian phenotypes. Future research should prioritize biomarkers (e.g. PER3 polymorphisms) to predict individual responses and optimize dosing regimens. 4.2. REV–ERBα/β synthetic ligands REV–ERBα and REV–ERBβ, nuclear receptors encoded by NR1D1 and NR1D2, are critical components of the circadian clock machinery. They repress BMAL1 transcription by competitively binding to ROR response elements (ROREs), counteracting RORα/γ-mediated activation and stabilizing the secondary feedback loop essential for circadian oscillation [ 21 , 68 ]. Synthetic ligands targeting these receptors have emerged as promising therapeutics for insomnia, particularly in cases driven by circadian misalignment and metabolic dysregulation. The REV–ERB agonist SR9009 enhances circadian amplitude by selectively binding to REV–ERBα/β, suppressing BMAL1 transcription, and phase-advancing peripheral clocks. In jet-lagged mice, SR9009 reduced sleep latency by 25% and increased non-REM sleep duration by 15%, accompanied by upregulated PER2 and CRY1 expression in the SCN [ 88 ]. Similarly, SR9011, another agonist, improved sleep consolidation in a rodent shift work model, decreasing nighttime hyperactivity by 40% and restoring hepatic BMAL1 rhythmicity [ 89 ]. These effects are linked to REV–ERB’s dual role in circadian and metabolic regulation. For example, SR9009 normalized glucose tolerance and reduced oxidative stress markers (e.g. malondialdehyde) in the SCN of sleep-deprived mice, suggesting neuroprotective benefits [ 90 ]. Combining REV–ERB ligands with behavioral interventions may enhance therapeutic outcomes. In a pilot trial, co-administration of SR9009 with timed blue light exposure in shift workers improved circadian alignment, reducing Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) scores by 35% over 4 weeks [ 91 ]. Emerging agonists like LY3045698, a brain-penetrant REV–ERBα ligand, selectively repress SCN BMAL1 without altering hepatic gene expression in primates, offering a strategy to minimize metabolic side effects [ 42 ]. Current REV–ERB agonists face pharmacokinetic challenges, including poor oral bioavailability (15–20% in rodents) and short half-lives (∼2 h for SR9009), requiring frequent dosing [ 92 ]. To overcome these limitations, several strategies are being explored. These include the development of prodrug formulations to enhance absorption and stability, the use of nanoparticle-based delivery systems to improve bioavailability and prolong half-life, and the design of novel brain-penetrant agonists with optimized pharmacokinetic properties [ 93 ]. Additionally, REV–ERBα knockout mice exhibit impaired antiviral immunity, raising concerns about infection risk in long-term human use [ 94 ]. In summary, REV–ERBα/β synthetic ligands represent a mechanistically grounded approach to circadian insomnia. 4.3. Dopamine receptor modulators Dopamine, a key neurotransmitter in the mesolimbic and nigrostriatal pathways, regulates arousal, reward processing, and circadian rhythms [ 95 ]. Dysregulation of dopaminergic signaling, particularly  via  D1 and D2 receptors, is implicated in hyperarousal states and sleep fragmentation in insomnia [ 96 ]. Dopamine receptor modulators (DRMs) aim to restore circadian alignment by targeting these receptors, offering a novel approach for insomnia with comorbid neuropsychiatric conditions. Dopamine receptor partial agonists, such as aripiprazole, stabilize dopaminergic tone by balancing D2 receptor activation and inhibition. In rodent models of circadian disruption, aripiprazole reduced nighttime hyperactivity by 30% and increased non-REM sleep duration by 20% through upregulation of PER2 expression in the SCN [ 97 ]. Similarly, cariprazine, a D3-preferring agonist, improved sleep continuity in mice with genetic CLOCK mutations, likely  via  modulation of GABAergic neurotransmission in the thalamus [ 98 ]. Antagonists of dopamine reuptake transporters, such as modafinil, indirectly enhance dopaminergic signaling by increasing extracellular dopamine levels. While primarily used for excessive daytime sleepiness, low-dose modafinil (50 mg/day) advanced circadian phase by 1.5 h in shift workers with insomnia, correlating with increased BMAL1 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells [ 99 ]. Selective D1 receptor antagonists, such as ecopipam, showed mixed results. A 8-week randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study in 19 children with Tourette syndrome showed no significant improvement in tic severity with Ecopipam, indicating D1 receptor antagonism may be insufficient for symptom control [ 100 ]. Conversely, combined D2/D3 agonists like piribedil demonstrated promise in small cohorts, reducing nighttime awakenings by 40% in Parkinson’s disease-related insomnia [ 101 ]. DRMs are associated with dose-dependent side effects, including akathisia (15–20% with aripiprazole) and metabolic disturbances (e.g. weight gain with quetiapine) [ 102 ]. Long-term use of dopamine reuptake inhibitors like modafinil may exacerbate anxiety or tachyphylaxis, limiting chronic application [ 103 ]. Additionally, DRMs’ effects on reward pathways raise concerns about misuse potential in vulnerable populations. 4.4. GABAergic drugs GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid), the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system, not only suppresses neuronal excitability to promote sleep but also interacts with circadian clock genes to modulate sleep–wake rhythms. Emerging evidence suggests that GABAergic drugs may exert therapeutic effects on insomnia by directly or indirectly influencing the expression and activity of core circadian clock components (e.g. CLOCK, BMAL1, PER, CRY). This section explores the molecular interplay between GABAergic signaling and circadian clock genes, highlighting implications for insomnia treatment. SCN, the master circadian pacemaker, receives GABAergic inputs from interneurons and extra-SCN regions. GABA(A) receptor activation in the SCN regulates phase shifts and stabilizes circadian oscillations. Zolpidem is clinically effective for the short-term treatment of sleep-onset insomnia, as demonstrated in numerous clinical trials. Beyond its sedative–hypnotic effects, experimental research in rodents suggests it may also influence circadian timing by enhancing SCN neuronal synchronization and upregulating PER2 expression [ 104 ]. Similarly, benzodiazepines (e.g. diazepam) modulate BMAL1 transcription in the SCN  via  GABA(A)-mediated inhibition of glutamatergic signaling, restoring rhythmicity in mice with Clock gene mutations [ 105 ]. These findings underscore GABA’s dual role in both acute sedation and circadian resetting. GABAergic drugs influence peripheral circadian clocks through systemic effects. In the liver, eszopiclone administration increases CRY1 expression and represses CLOCK-dependent metabolic genes, aligning peripheral clocks with the central SCN rhythm [ 106 ]. This synchronization improves sleep quality in patients with metabolic syndrome-associated insomnia. Additionally, GABA(B) receptor agonists (e.g. baclofen) enhance REV–ERBα activity in the prefrontal cortex, a region critical for sleep initiation, by suppressing BMAL1-mediated glutamatergic hyperactivity [ 107 ]. Such interactions suggest that GABAergic agents can target both central and peripheral circadian pathways to mitigate insomnia. Beyond these effects, increasing evidence reveals that GABAergic signaling and circadian genes form reciprocal regulatory loops. For example, GABA(A) receptor activity in SCN neurons shows circadian rhythmicity, which is partly driven by BMAL1/CLOCK-dependent transcription of GABA receptor subunits [ 108 ]. Conversely, pharmacological enhancement of GABAergic tone can alter the phase and amplitude of PER1/2 expression, thereby feeding back to reset circadian oscillations [ 109 ]. Moreover, CRY1 has been shown to modulate GABA(A) receptor trafficking in thalamic neurons, linking circadian clock gene function directly with inhibitory synaptic transmission [ 74 ]. These bidirectional interactions highlight that GABAergic drugs not only promote sedation but also fine-tune circadian rhythmicity at the molecular level. While GABAergic drugs rapidly alleviate insomnia symptoms, their long-term use may disrupt circadian plasticity. Chronic benzodiazepine exposure reduces PER3 expression in human fibroblasts, correlating with diminished circadian amplitude and non-REM sleep fragmentation [ 110 ]. Conversely, low-dose zaleplon preserves PER1/2 rhythmicity in shift workers, demonstrating subtype-specific effects on clock genes [ 111 ]. However, dependency risks and tolerance—linked to epigenetic modifications of CLOCK promoter regions—limit their utility [ 112 ]. 4.5. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) TCM offers a holistic approach to insomnia treatment by targeting both circadian rhythm regulation and systemic balance. Emerging evidence suggests that TCM interventions, including herbal formulations and acupuncture, may modulate circadian clock gene expression and restore sleep–wake cycles through multi-pathway mechanisms. This section explores the potential of TCM in circadian-aligned insomnia therapy. Several TCM herbs and formulations have demonstrated circadian-regulatory properties. Suanzaoren Decoction, a classic formula for insomnia, upregulates PER2 and CRY1 expression in the SCN of sleep-deprived rodents, enhancing circadian amplitude and consolidating non-REM sleep [ 113 ]. A randomized controlled trial of Suanzaoren Decoction in patients with insomnia showed significant improvements in subjective sleep quality compared to placebo [ 114 ]. Mechanistically, Studies have indicated that Jiaotai Pills can alleviate insomnia and promote sleep by inhibiting substances related to wakefulness promotion (Glu, GAT3, GAT1, GABA-T) and increasing substances related to sleep promotion (GABAA, GABAB, GAD) [ 115 ]. Anmeidan modulates the cAMP Response Element-Binding Protein (CREB)/Per signaling pathway, upregulates biomolecular clock proteins Bmal1, Clock, Per1, and Cry1, and enhances the circadian rhythm of spontaneous activity in sleep-deprived rats [ 116 ]. Single herbs also exhibit circadian-specific effects. The sedative and hypnotic effects of PT in aged insomnia rats might be related to neuro, metabolism pathways, especially through GABAergic signaling pathway. It provided more effective herb choice for the treatment of senile insomnia [ 117 ]. Nobiletin, a polymethoxyflavonoid from citrus peel, improves memory loss and acts as a RORs agonist. Studies show it can modulate the circadian clock by regulating BMAL1, Per1, etc [ 118 ]. Studies have shown that for perimenopausal insomnia patients with the phlegm-heat syndrome, using the modified Wen Dan Decoction can help regulate neurotransmitters, modulate inflammatory factors, improve sex hormone levels, enhance sleep quality, and increase treatment effectiveness [ 119 ]. Acupuncture, a key TCM therapy, is effective for sleep disorders. Research indicates it can treat these disorders by regulating circadian clock genes [ 120 ]. In summary, circadian clock gene-targeted therapies represent a promising avenue for insomnia management by addressing the molecular underpinnings of circadian disruption. From melatonin receptor agonists and REV–ERB modulators to dopamine receptor regulators, GABAergic drugs, and Traditional Chinese Medicine, these approaches collectively illustrate the potential of circadian-aligned interventions. While each strategy has distinct advantages and limitations, together they highlight the translational significance of circadian biology in guiding personalized treatment options. A schematic overview of these therapeutic strategies and their representative mechanisms is provided in  Figure 2 . Figure 2. Molecular pathways linking circadian clock dysfunction to insomnia. This schematic summarizes current circadian-aligned therapeutic approaches, including melatonin receptor agonists (e.g. ramelteon, agomelatine, tasimelteon), REV–ERB agonists (e.g. SR9009, SR9011), dopamine receptor modulators, GABAergic drugs, and Traditional Chinese Medicine. Each class of therapy acts through distinct molecular mechanisms—ranging from MT1/MT2-mediated circadian alignment, BMAL1 suppression, dopaminergic arousal regulation, and GABA receptor–driven neural inhibition, to multi-target regulation by TCM. Representative advantages and limitations of each strategy are highlighted, providing an integrative overview of potential circadian-based interventions for insomnia. 5. Conclusion and future perspectives 5.1. Conclusion Insomnia, a pervasive sleep disorder with significant health implications, is increasingly recognized as a condition rooted in molecular dysregulation of circadian clock genes. This review synthesizes evidence highlighting the pivotal role of core circadian clock components—BMAL1, CLOCK, PER, CRY, and REV–ERBα/β—in orchestrating sleep–wake cycles and maintaining physiological homeostasis. Genetic polymorphisms, epigenetic modifications, and environmental disruptions in these genes contribute to circadian misalignment, hyperarousal states, and metabolic-inflammatory imbalances, all of which exacerbate insomnia. Mechanistically, clock genes regulate neurotransmitter systems (e.g. melatonin, serotonin, GABA, dopamine), mitochondrial function, and neuroimmune crosstalk, offering a molecular framework to explain sleep fragmentation and impaired sleep quality. Current therapeutic strategies targeting circadian pathways, such as melatonin receptor agonists (e.g. ramelteon, agomelatine), REV–ERB synthetic ligands (e.g. SR9009), and GABAergic drugs, demonstrate efficacy in specific subtypes of insomnia, particularly those linked to circadian disruption. However, limitations persist, including subtype-dependent responses, pharmacokinetic challenges, and long-term safety concerns. TCM interventions, such as Suanzaoren Decoction and acupuncture, show promise in modulating clock gene expression and restoring circadian rhythms, though further mechanistic validation is required ( Table 2 ). Future research directions and challenges To translate the promise of circadian medicine into clinical reality for insomnia treatment, future research must address several key priorities with a focus on biomarker-driven, personalized approaches: First, the discovery and validation of robust circadian biomarkers are essential for patient stratification. This includes identifying genetic variants beyond known polymorphisms (e.g. through large-scale pharmacogenomic studies) and utilizing physiological measures like dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) to predict individual response to timed light, melatonin, or novel clock-targeting drugs [ 121 ]. Critically, there is a pressing need for biomarker-driven clinical trials that stratify insomnia patients based on circadian phenotypes to better match individuals with targeted chronotherapies and objectively measure treatment efficacy. Second, the integration of multi-omics technologies (e.g. transcriptomics, metabolomics) is needed to define molecular sub-types of insomnia and uncover novel therapeutic targets within the circadian–immune–metabolic axis [ 122 ]. Third, overcoming the pharmacokinetic limitations of next-generation compounds (e.g. REV–ERB agonists) requires innovative strategies, such as developing prodrug formulations and nanoparticle-based delivery systems to enhance bioavailability and half life [ 60 ]. Fourth, there is a critical shortage of long-term safety and efficacy data for most circadian-targeted therapies. Prospective longitudinal studies and real-world evidence are urgently needed to assess risks like receptor desensitization and the long-term impact of circadian modulation on overall health [ 123 ]. Finally, the mechanistic validation of TCM interventions necessitates a modern research framework. This can be achieved through a multi-level approach: (1) Computational target identification to pinpoint active compounds and their circadian targets; (2) Preclinical models to verify effects on core clock genes and proteins; (3) Multi-omics analyses to characterize system-level responses; and (4) Biomarker-driven clinical trials incorporating molecular endpoints and objective sleep measures [ 124 ]. Embracing this comprehensive, evidence-based, and biomarker-driven roadmap will be crucial for developing precise and effective chronotherapeutic interventions for insomnia [ 41 ].

Introduction Sleep is widespread among homeothermic animals and has important impacts on cognition, memory formation, 1  brain plasticity, 2  insulin release and response, 3  temperature regulation, 4  and immune maintenance. 5  However, amid the rapid pace of modern society and the rising trend of an aging population, sleep disorders are increasingly prevalent among a growing number of individuals. Sleep disorders currently affect an estimated one-third of the world’s population, representing a significant and growing public health concern. 6  A Korean retrospective cohort study revealed that the prevalence of sleep disorders increased from 7.62% in 2011 to 14.41% in 2020, nearly doubling over the decade. 7  Long-term sleep disorders can increase the risk of obesity, 8  diabetes, 9  cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, 10  dementia, 11  and other diseases. Sleep disorders not only significantly diminish the quality of life for individuals but also place a substantial societal burden. Therefore, sleep science has become one of the hot topics in contemporary research. Sleep is a natural, cyclical physiological state characterized by the disappearance of various conscious voluntary behaviors for a period, as well as decreased responsiveness to external stimuli. One important feature is the ability of the brain to transition rapidly from a state of sleep to wakefulness. 12  The two-process model 13  is currently the most widely accepted theory in sleep-wake regulation. This model proposes that sleep is the result of the interaction and integration of sleep-wake homeostasis (Process S) and the circadian rhythm system (Process C). Electroencephalogram (EEG) signals are the sum of synchronized excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials of cortical neurons, which are fundamental in sleep research. In EEG studies, the spectral features of wakefulness span alpha (8–12 Hz), beta (12–35 Hz), and gamma (>35 Hz) bands, with beta and gamma dominating during active cognition and alpha dominating during a relaxed state 14  (Fig.  1 ). Based on different manifestations in EEG and electromyograms (EMG), sleep can be divided into nonrapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. 15 , 16  In NREM sleep, the delta band (0.5–4 Hz) is the predominant oscillation, especially during the slow-wave sleep (SWS)/NREM stage, whereas the theta band (4–8 Hz) is the characteristic rhythm during REM sleep. 15 , 16  Organisms acquire nutrients from their surroundings, converting them through digestion, absorption, and metabolism processes into usable energy for tissues and cells, thereby sustaining vital life functions. Energy metabolism encompasses the coordinated processes of energy production, allocation, storage, and utilization. The primary role of cellular energy metabolism lies in synthesizing adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the universal currency of biological energy. This process mainly occurs in the mitochondria through oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). 17 , 18  Additionally, it contributes to cell signaling, 19 , 20  neural signal transmission, 21 , 22  hormone synthesis and secretion, 23  maintenance of body temperature, 24  and normal functioning of the immune system. 25  The energy metabolism of the brain is exceptionally active; despite representing just 2% of body weight, it consumes 20% of the body’s total energy. 22  This high energy consumption is predominantly dedicated to powering neuronal signaling and maintaining ionic gradients across cell membranes, underscoring the profound interdependence between neural function and metabolic support. The alpha band (8–12] Hz is observed during relaxed wakefulness. The theta band (4-8] Hz is linked to deep relaxation. The delta band [0.5–4] Hz is most prominent during NREM sleep and is associated with reduced consciousness. (a, b] indicates all numbers greater than “a” and less than or equal to “b”, where “(“ is exclusive while “]” is inclusive There is a bidirectional relationship between sleep and energy metabolism. Different species require different amounts of sleep. In fact, sleep duration is not influenced by brain size or cognitive abilities. Instead, it is related to the ecological niche and feeding requirements of the species, 26  indicating that the balance of sleep-wakefulness plays a role in food acquisition and energy expenditure. NREM sleep, particularly SWS, represents a fundamental state of energy conservation and restoration. This function is directly driven by the brain’s dominant electrophysiological pattern: synchronized, low-frequency, high-amplitude oscillations in the delta band (0.5–4 Hz). 27  These slow waves reflect a highly coordinated, oscillating pattern of neuronal silence and activity, which lowers the brain’s metabolic demand. Concurrently, this period is marked by a significant decline in both cerebral and core body temperatures, a result of reduced thermoregulatory set-point. 28  This systemic cooling further contributes to a substantial reduction in the overall metabolic rate and energy expenditure, allowing for the replenishment of energy stores and critical cellular repair processes. In contrast, REM sleep is a period of active energy consumption and redistribution. 29  Despite a state of muscle atonia that paralyzes the body, the brain’s metabolic rate surges to levels matching wakefulness. This high energy cost is directed toward functions essential for higher-order cognition, particularly the reactivation and consolidation of memories and the intricate processing of emotions. 30  To fuel this intense cerebral activity, energy is strategically diverted away from nonessential somatic functions. 30 Synaptic homeostasis also provides a strong link between energy metabolism and sleep regulation. Synaptic transmission is one of the most energy-costly processes in the brain. 31  The current study indicates that sleep-dependent synaptic downscaling occurs, 32  a phenomenon that helps to explain the energy conservation observed during this period. In addition, a key piece of evidence is that the potentiation of excitatory synapses within the prefrontal cortex (PFC) has been demonstrated to promote longer NREM sleep duration and higher delta wave power, which are hallmarks of deep sleep. 33  Consequently, a drop in cellular energy metabolism disrupts the precise modulation of synaptic strength, a mechanism that supports both learning during wakefulness and restorative processes during sleep. In this review, we explore the role of energy metabolism in the initiation of the sleep-wake cycle, as well as the interplay between specific brain nuclei and neurotransmitters; examine how energy metabolism influences the sleep-wake cycle through sleep-wake homeostasis, the circadian rhythm system and the different types of cells; analyze the connection between energy dysmetabolism-related diseases and the increased risk of sleep disorders; summarize medications that simultaneously enhance energy metabolism and improve sleep; and propose the potential of using drugs that enhance energy metabolism as a novel therapeutic approach for sleep disorder intervention. The initiation of the sleep-wake cycle Traditionally, sleep was misconceived as a passive state of neural quiescence; however, extensive experimental evidence has firmly established it as a complex, actively regulated process orchestrated by the central nervous system. 12 , 34  The seamless progression of the sleep-wake cycle depends on a dynamic balance, maintained by complex interactions and mutual inhibition among numerous neural nuclei and neurotransmitters/neuropeptides in the brain, which influence the initiation and maintenance of sleep and wakefulness. Homeostatic regulation of sleep-wake nuclei in the sleep-wake cycle The sleep-wake cycle is governed by a complex interplay of specialized neuronal circuits (Fig.  2 ). The classical ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) consists of dorsal and ventral pathways driving arousal. The dorsal pathway originating from pedunculopontine tegmental nuclei (PPT)/laterodorsal tegmental nuclei (LDT) cholinergic neurons activates thalamocortical circuits for sensory integration, while the ventral pathway integrates inputs from locus coeruleus (LC) norepinephrinergic, dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) serotonergic, ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopaminergic, tuberomammillary nucleus (TMN) histaminergic, and lateral hypothalamus (LH) orexinergic nuclei to sustain prolonged wakefulness. Modern optogenetic/chemogenetic studies have expanded this framework by identifying novel arousal-promoting populations, including glutamatergic neurons in the paraventricular thalamus (PVT), medial parabrachial nucleus (MPB), and basal forebrain (BF), as well as GABAergic interneurons across midbrain and forebrain regions. These systems counterbalance sleep-active nuclei such as the ventrolateral preoptic area (VLPO) hypothalamic region, whose inhibitory projections to ARAS components are critical for transitioning into NREM sleep via GABA/galanin release. Thalamic networks further regulate this equilibrium through the centromedial thalamus (CMT) nuclei mediating sleep recovery and the thalamic reticular nuclei (TRN) circuits generating sleep spindles. REM sleep is regulated by a specialized subnetwork involving neurons in the sublaterodorsal tegmentum nucleus (SLD) that drive state transitions while being constrained by GABAergic gatekeepers in the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG) and dorsal deep mesencephalic nucleus (dDpMe). This multilayered system achieves homeostatic regulation through reciprocal interactions between wake-promoting, NREM sleep-promoting, and REM sleep-promoting circuits. The dorsal pathway allows the thalamus to process signals related to sensation, motor responses, and cognition, with minimal impact on wakefulness duration. 40  However, an impaired ventral pathway can significantly reduce wakefulness duration. 41 With the advent of technologies such as calcium imaging, optogenetics, and chemogenetics, it has become possible to monitor and modulate specific neuronal populations. An increasing number of nuclei have been identified as contributors to arousal, including glutamatergic neurons in the VTA, 42  BF, 43 , 44  PVT, 45  and MPB, 46  as well as GABAergic neurons in the BF, 43  LH, 47  SC, 48  and VP. 49  In addition, the ventromedial thalamic nucleus (VM), 50  dorsal medial thalamus (DMT), 51  and posterior parietal cortex (PtA) 52  have also been shown to promote arousal. Ren et al. recently revealed that GABAergic neurons expressing GAD2 in the midbrain dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN 2GAD ) are activated during wakefulness and can inhibit excessive arousal under both physiological and stress conditions. 53  This means that the state of wakefulness is finely controlled by the balanced activity of wake-promoting neurons and wake-limiting neurons (Table  1 ). hypothalamus. 54  The VLPO sends inhibitory projections to several arousal-promoting neuronal populations, 55  including PPT/LDT cholinergic neurons, 55  LC norepinephrinergic neurons, 56  DRN serotonergic neurons, 56  midbrain dopaminergic neurons, 56  TMN histaminergic neurons, 57  and LH orexinergic neurons. 58  By inhibiting these arousal-related neurons, the VLPO promotes sleep. In the VLPO, neurons release inhibitory neurotransmitters such as galanin and GABA and are mainly active during sleep. 57 , 59  The activation of the VLPO is positively correlated with sleep duration, and its destruction leads to a reduction in NREM sleep time. 54 , 60  Notably, glucose can activate VLPO neurons to induce slow-wave sleep, suggesting a link between energy metabolism and sleep, 61  which in part explains the phenomenon of postprandial sleepiness. The thalamus has a dual role in the regulation of sleep and wakefulness. It has been mentioned above that thalamic nuclei such as PVT, VM, and DMT are involved in the regulation of wakefulness. CMT neurons in the thalamus can not only induce NREM-wake transitions but also promote sleep recovery. 62  By using simultaneous functional MRI (fMRI) and EEG, Song et al. demonstrated that the thalamus has an important function in the initiation and maintenance of sleep. 63  In addition, sleep spindles (bursts of activity at 7–15 Hz during NREM sleep) are generated by the interaction between thalamic reticular nuclei (TRN) and thalamocortical neurons. 64  Recent studies have shown that GABAergic neurons 47  and cholinergic neurons 65  in the TRN, as well as neurotensinergic neurons within a thalamo-amygdala circuit involving the posterior thalamus and the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeA), 66  can promote NREM sleep. Combining optogenetic activation, optrode recording, and in vitro physiology, Xu et al. found that activation of somatostatin-positive (SOM + ) GABAergic neurons in the BF can promote NREM sleep. 43  Melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH) neurons in the LH are also involved in the regulation of NREM sleep. Selective ablation of MCH neurons in the LH resulted in decreased NREM sleep and unchanged REM sleep. 67  Interestingly, prolonged inhibition of LH elicits a unique NREM sleep state with enhanced slow-wave activity and REM sleep suppression, an effect not observed following selective orexin or MCH neuron inactivation, pointing to the existence of additional sleepregulatory neurons in this region. 68  Chronic optogenetic activation of MCH neurons (over 24 hours) can increase both NREM and REM sleep. 69  Furthermore, multiple other neuronal populations have been implicated in the regulation of NREM sleep. These include cortical nNOS/NK1 neurons 70 ; somatostatin-positive cortical interneurons 71 ; adenosine A 2A  receptor neurons in the striatum, 72  NAc, 73 , 74  and olfactory tubercle (OT) 75 ; parafacial zone (PZ) GABAergic neurons 76 – 78 ; neurotensin (NTS)-expressing glutamatergic neurons in the vlPAG 79 ;  and neurotensinergic neurons in the SLD of the pontine. 80 REM sleep nuclei REM sleep nuclei contain two types of mutually antagonistic neurons. 81  One type of neuron can inhibit wakefulness and NREM sleep and promote the initiation and maintenance of REM sleep. The SLD is a key nucleus for REM sleep. 81 , 82  The SLD contains glutamatergic, GABAergic, and possibly cholinergic neurons, which are strongly activated during REM sleep and wakefulness. 83 , 84  Pharmacologic activation or disinhibition of SLD can increase REM sleep duration. 85  LH orexin neurons can also play a role in stabilizing REM sleep by modulating the SLD. 86  GABAergic neurons in the ventral medulla, 87  dorsomedial medulla (dmM), 88  LH, 89  and zona incerta (ZI), 90  MCH neurons in the LH, 91 , 92  and neurons in the retrosplenial cortex (RSC) 93  have all been shown to promote REM sleep. Recently, Hasegawa et al. found that basolateral amygdala (BLA) dopamine signaling from the VTA is significant for the initiation of REM sleep. 94  The cholinergic neurons of the PPT/LDT, along with the majority of glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons, are also believed to be involved in the initiation and maintenance of REM sleep. 83 , 95 Another group of neurons acts as gatekeepers for REM sleep and is primarily located in the vlPAG 96  and dDpMe, 97  consisting mainly of GABAergic neurons. The majority of vlPAG/dDpMe GABA  neurons exhibit the highest activity during wakefulness, decrease their activity during NREM sleep and are almost inactive during REM sleep, while a small subset of neurons show the greatest activity during REM sleep. 96  Activation of vlPAG/dDpMe GABA  neurons using optogenetic or chemogenetic approaches can significantly inhibit REM sleep. 96 , 98 Under normal conditions, the neural circuits of wakefulness-promoting and sleep-promoting nuclei, along with their neurotransmitters/neuropeptides, interact to maintain homeostasis between wakefulness and sleep (Fig.  3a ). Impairment of any one of these associated nuclei results in sleep-wake disturbances. The “flip-flop switch” theory 37 , 99  provides a good explanation for the rapid transition between sleep and wakefulness cycles. The LH orexinergic neurons serve as a critical “switch button” for the transition. 37 , 99  When their excitability increases, they promote the excitation of almost all wakefulness-promoting nuclei, which in turn inhibit the VLPO, thereby terminating sleep and inducing wakefulness. 99 , 100  Conversely, when their excitability decreases, the inhibitory effect of these wake-promoting nuclei on the VLPO is reduced, which terminates wakefulness and initiates sleep. 37 , 99  If the activity of LH orexin neurons is reduced or absent, it severely affects the initiation of wakefulness, leading to narcolepsy (which is discussed in detail below) 101 , 102  (Fig.  3b ). Fatal familial insomnia (FFI) also serves as a model disease in sleep physiopathology, characterized by the loss of sleep spindles and K-complexes. 103  The D178N mutation of the prion protein-encoding gene (PRNP) causes the normal prion protein to misfold into a pathogenic form, leading to abnormal accumulation of pathogenic protein in the thalamus, particularly in the anterior (A) and dorsomedian (DM) thalamic nuclei, and inferior olivary nuclei 104 , 105  (Fig.  3c ). The TRN is essential for the generation of sleep spindles , 64  and the DM receives afferents from the oral pole of the TRN. 106  Therefore, degeneration of the DM may underlie the loss of spindling activity in FFI. 103 Fig. 3 The wakefulness and sleep initiation systems coordinate and constrain each other.  a  In the normal sleep-wake cycle, the wakefulness and sleep systems counteract each other to maintain homeostasis.  b  In narcolepsy, the reduced or absent activity of orexin neurons in the arousal system of the LH weakens its excitatory effects, leading to a more stable inhibitory effect from the sleep system.  c  Fatal familial insomnia is pathologically characterized by the abnormal deposition of prion proteins in the thalamus, leading to neuronal degeneration, vacuole formation, and gliosis in that region. This results in a weakened inhibitory effect of the sleep system and, correspondingly, an enhanced excitatory effect of the wakefulness system. LC locus coeruleus, DRN dorsal raphe nucleus, PPT pedunculopontine tegmental, LDT laterodorsal tegmental, TMN tuberomammillary nucleus, LH lateral hypothalamus, BF basal forebrain, VLPO ventrolateral preoptic area, NAc nucleus accumbens Sleep-wake neurotransmitters/neuropeptides in the sleep-wake cycle The sleep-wake cycle is a complex physiologic process orchestrated by multiple neurotransmitters and neuropeptides. Central cholinergic systems play pivotal roles in maintaining wakefulness through acetylcholine-mediated activation of nicotinic and muscarinic receptors, with marked increases during both REM sleep and waking states (Table  2 ). Wakefulness represents a distinct behavioral state characterized by low-voltage high-frequency EEG patterns (α-γ bands) and postural stability, maintained via cholinergic projections from the basal forebrain to neocortical regions and the brainstem reticular activating system. 107  Serotonergic projections from the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) exhibit a dual role: while 5-HT neuronal activity peaks during active waking and may suppress REM sleep via G i /G s  coupled receptor signaling, recent studies highlight its bidirectional modulation of sleep regulation through tonic/burst firing patterns in distinct brain regions. 108  Dopaminergic pathways contribute to arousal by activating D1-type receptors, with dysregulation linked to altered NREM/REM architecture. Arousal is a broad neurophysiological concept encompassing sustained cortical network activation, primarily regulated by the dopaminergic pathway in the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra and the histaminergic pathway in the hypothalamus circuits , 54 , 109 ,  Noradrenergic output from the locus coeruleus (LC) exhibits phasic activity during waking via α 1 /α 2  receptor signaling, 110  while histaminergic neurons maintain sustained alertness through H 1  receptor-mediated cortical excitation. 54  Alertness denotes an optimized sensory processing threshold reflecting heightened vigilance, primarily mediated by histaminergic neurons in the tuberomammillary nucleus of the hypothalamus. These neurons directly excite corticothalamic circuits through H 1  receptor activation. 111  Simultaneously, orexin neurons in the LH are active during wakefulness and essential for stabilizing the wake state and sustaining alertness by inhibiting sleep-active regions, such as the ventrolateral preoptic area (VLPO), and activating monoaminergic nuclei. Loss of orexin-producing neurons in humans results in narcolepsy, a disorder characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness and sudden transitions between wakefulness and sleep. Inhibitory GABAergic signaling via GABA A  receptors provides counterbalancing mechanisms to modulate excitatory drives. Emerging evidence underscores the interdependence between these systems and mitochondrial energetics, as ATP-dependent vesicular uptake and release of neurotransmitters rely on axonal mitochondrial trafficking, a process whose dysfunction disrupts neurochemical homeostasis and sleep regulation equilibrium. More strikingly, long-term knockout of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors M1 and M3 nearly eliminates REM sleep, leaving it at barely detectable levels. 125  Furthermore, brain-wide functional ultrasonic imaging and cell-type-specific calcium imaging combined with optogenetics have shown that during NREM sleep, cortical ignition (a brain process related to conscious awareness in humans and nonhuman primates) is strongly suppressed due to reduced cholinergic modulation and rapid inhibition of cortical responses. 126 Serotonin/5-hydroxytryptamine exhibits bidirectional regulation of the sleep-wake cycle Serotonin/5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) was initially thought to be a vasoconstrictor. Subsequent research has confirmed that serotonin (5-HT) is also distributed in the brain. 127  Serotonin (5-HT) neurons are mainly distributed in the DRN of the brainstem 128  and are involved in the regulation of physiological functions such as sleep, 108 , 129  mood, 130  learning and memory, 131  pain, 132  and movement. 133  As a monoamine neurotransmitter, serotonin (5-HT) is derived from tryptophan through the action of tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH) and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC). 134  Serotonin (5-HT) synthesized within neurons is transported from the cytoplasm into synaptic vesicles via vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), and it is subsequently released into the synaptic cleft upon neuronal activation. Concurrently, the serotonin (5-HT) reuptake transporter (SERT), located in the presynaptic membrane, facilitates the reuptake of serotonin (5-HT) from the synaptic cleft back into the neuron, 135  where it is subsequently metabolized by monoamine oxidase (MAO) located on the outer membrane of mitochondria. Seven 5-HT receptors have been previously identified. The 5-HT 3  receptor is the only receptor that functions as a ligand-gated ion channel receptor, while all other types of 5-HT receptors are G protein-coupled receptors. 136  The 5-HT 1  and 5-HT 5  receptors primarily couple with G i  proteins, leading to the inhibition of AC activity. 137  In contrast, the 5-HT 4 , 5-HT 6 , and 5-HT 7  receptors predominantly couple with G s  proteins, resulting in the activation of AC activity. 137  Additionally, 5-HT 2  receptors mainly couple with G q  proteins, which activate the activity of PLC. 138 Serotonin (5-HT) has a complex bidirectional role in the regulation of the sleep-wake cycle. Earlier studies have found that impairments or reductions in the production of the 5-HT pathway lead to decreased sleep in rats or cats, 139  suggesting that 5-HT has sleep-promoting effects. However, several subsequent studies have reported that 5-HT neurons in the DRN are most active during active waking, significantly less active during NREM sleep, and cease firing during REM sleep. 140 – 142  Reducing the activity of these neurons can induce sleep. 143  Consequently, the paradigm of 5-HT shifts toward its arousal function. 144  In recent years, an increasing number of studies have provided evidence supporting the notion that 5-HT also plays a role in promoting sleep. Tryptophan hydroxylase 2 (Tph2) deficiency affects the synthesis of 5-HT in the brain. reward, 151  behavior, and emotion. 152  Dopamine is primarily synthesized from tyrosine, 153  with tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) playing crucial functions in this process. 154  Similar to 5-HT, synthetic dopamine can enter synaptic vesicles via VMAT2 and be released into the synaptic cleft upon neuronal activation. 154  The dopamine transporter, located in identified, namely, D 1 , D 2 , D 3 , D 4,  and D 5 . 156 , 157  As G protein-coupled receptors, they are categorized into two classes. 158  Specifically, D 1  and D 5  receptors are classified as neurons in the VTA and DRN significantly contribute to arousal. 160 – 162  Systemic administration of selective D 1  receptor agonists can induce arousal and suppress REM sleep in rats. 163  Similarly, selective activation of D 1 -expressing neurons in the striatum or nucleus accumbens (NAc) using optogenetics can induce a rapid transition from NREM sleep to wakefulness, while the decrease in wakefulness and increased NREM and REM sleep but decreased EEG delta power during NREM sleep, especially during the early stage of the active phase. 166 Noradrenaline promotes wakefulness In the brain, NA primarily originates from the locus coeruleus (LC) in the pons. As a monoamine neurotransmitter, NA synthesized within neurons is also transported into vesicles by VMAT2 and is released upon the triggering of an action potential. 167  The norepinephrine transporter (NET) located in the presynaptic membrane can also regulate NA release and reuptake. 168 , 169  NA in neurons is mainly metabolized by the MAO pathway. 170  NA receptors are all G protein-coupled receptors, including three pharmacological receptor types, α 1 , α 2,  and β, each of which can be further divided into three subtypes according to their structure and function. 171  The α 1  receptors are primarily coupled with G q  protein to promote the activation of PLC; the α 2  receptors are mainly coupled to G i  protein, which inhibits AC; the β receptors are predominantly coupled to G s  proteins and play an activating role in AC 171 ; β 2 172  and β 3 173  receptors are also coupled to G i .  receptor antagonists can increase the duration of sleep in a rat model of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). 174  α 2  receptor agonists can inhibit the release of NA, reduce arousal, and exert sedative effects. 175  In addition, a rare and less stable mutant of the β 1  subtype receptor can increase arousal and reduce sleep duration in humans and mice. 176  Recent findings indicate that and H 2  receptors are widely expressed in both the brain and peripheral tissues 187 ; the H 3  receptor is primarily expressed in the brain, 188  while the H 4  receptor is mainly expressed in However, it is rarely expressed in the brain and primarily functions in peripheral tissues to regulate immune responses. 189 Orexin (hypocretin) is a critical homeostatic regulator of the sleep–wake cycle In 1998, the research teams of Yanagisawa 205  and Sutcliffe 206  simultaneously discovered orexin (hypocretin) neuropeptides. Orexin consists of two types, orexin-A and orexin-B, which are derived from a common precursor peptide, prepro-orexin (PPO). 205  Orexin is primarily synthesized by neurons in the lateral hypothalamus (LH), which can modulate the level of arousal to suit behavioral needs and regulate energy balance. 207  For example, the orexin system is activated in response to stress and emotion, 208 , 209  and it is suppressed in response to high glucose levels. 210  Orexin has two receptors, the orexin-1 receptor (OX 1 R) and the orexin-2 receptor (OX 2 R), which are mainly coupled to the G q  protein. 205  When orexin receptors are activated, they can promote the activity of PLC. 211  Orexin-A binds to OX 1 R and OX 2 R with similar affinity, whereas orexin-B binds OX 2 R with higher affinity than OX 1 R. 205  It is worth noting that orexin functions not merely as a wakefulness-promoting neuropeptide but also as a critical homeostatic regulator of the sleep-wake cycle. Through gating state transitions, reinforcing sustained arousal, and preventing pathological intrusions of NREM or REM sleep into wakefulness, orexin ensures the coherence and stability of vigilance states rather than simply triggering transient arousal. 212  Orexinergic neurons in the LH exert excitatory modulation of ascending arousal systems via projections to wake-promoting nuclei, including the noradrenergic LC, histaminergic TMN, and cholinergic BF. 100  Concurrently, orexin exerts an inhibitory influence over sleep-promoting nuclei, particularly the VLPO, thus consolidating the stability of vigilance states and impeding aberrant state transitions. 213  Orexin activity gradually decreases as sleep depth increases, promoting the transition of NREM sleep to its deeper stages and reducing abnormal arousal during NREM sleep. 99 , 214  In the later phase of NREM sleep, orexin activity decreases further, coordinating the transition from NREM sleep to REM sleep. 215 The stabilizing function of orexin is exemplified by narcolepsy type 1, characterized by autoimmune-mediated or sporadic degeneration of orexin neurons. 216  Narcolepsy is classified into two primary subtypes. Type 1 narcolepsy is defined by excessive daytime sleepiness accompanied by cataplexy, which distinguishes it from type 2 narcolepsy, where typical cataplexy is absent. 217  Notably, it has been established that the occurrence of type 1 narcolepsy in humans is caused by the loss of orexin neurons. 101 , 218  Given that loss of muscle tone is a defining feature of REM sleep, this points to an essential role for orexin in the regulation and stability of REM sleep. Although orexin neurons are silent during REM sleep, they provide robust excitatory drive to REM-off neurons during wakefulness. 219  This arrangement ensures that when the orexin system is intact, REM sleep is effectively prevented from intruding into the awake state. In the absence of orexin, the excitatory drive to REM-off neurons that normally stabilizes wakefulness is lost, blurring the boundary between arousal and REM sleep and giving rise to the characteristic episodes of cataplexy. Glutamate and its role in the sleep-wake cycle Glutamate (Glu) is the most abundant nonessential amino acid in humans. It serves not only as a key building block for protein synthesis but also as the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system (CNS) 220  while simultaneously participating in a variety of metabolic pathways. 221  Within neurons, α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) generated via the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle can be used to produce glutamate, enabling a rapid response to the demands of synaptic transmission. 222  Approximately 90% of the glutamate released by neurons into the synaptic cleft is taken up by excitatory amino acid transporters (EAATs) located on the membrane of astrocytes. 223 , 224  This glutamate is then converted into glutamine under the catalysis of glutamine synthetase (GS), enabling the “storage and regeneration” of glutamate in the brain through the glutamate-glutamine cycle. Glutamate receptors are classified into two major categories: ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) and metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs). 225  Different functional subgroups make up the family of iGluRs, including N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptors, kainate receptors, and GluD receptors. 226  These receptors can directly regulate the opening of ion channels and rapidly mediate excitatory synaptic transmission. Based on amino acid sequence homology and signaling pathways, mGluRs are classified into 3 groups, which consist of 8 subtypes: mGluR1 to mGluR8. 227  Group I mGluRs (mGluR1, mGluR5) couple to Gq proteins and exert an excitatory effect on downstream signaling pathways. Group II mGluRs (mGluR2, mGluR3) and Group III mGluRs (mGluR4, mGluR6, mGluR7, mGluR8) both couple to Gi proteins; they inhibit the presynaptic release of glutamate and thereby participate in negative feedback regulation. 227  Glutamatergic signaling is involved in the regulation of the sleep-wake cycle, 228  and human studies have revealed that this signaling dynamically changes throughout the sleep-wake cycle. 229 , 230  Glutamatergic neurons located in the brainstem reticular formation exhibit notably higher activity during wakefulness and REM sleep. 46 , 83 , 84 γ-Aminobutyric acid and its role in sleep γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter and has a significant role in promoting sleep. 231 , 232  GABA is synthesized by glutamate in the cytoplasm of presynaptic neurons through glutamate decarboxylase (GAD). 233  GABA is widely distributed in the brain, and when it binds to receptors, it can inhibit the response of neurons to excitatory neurotransmitters such as norepinephrine, serotonin, acetylcholine, histamine, and dopamine. 234  GABA has two receptor types in the central nervous system: GABA A  and GABA B . The GABA A  receptor is a ligand-gated chloride channel located at the synapse that mediates rapid inhibition. 235  The GABA B  receptor is a G i  protein-coupled metabolic receptor that reduces neuronal Ca 2+  influx and K +  efflux by inhibiting cAMP signaling, resulting in slower inhibitory transmission. 236  The GABA A  receptor is composed of five subunits. Currently, humans have 19 different GABA A  receptor subunits ( α 1-6 ,  β 1-3 ,  γ 1-3 ,  δ ,  ε ,  π ,  θ , and  ρ 1-3 ), which can randomly combine to form GABA A  subtypes with different physiological characteristics. 235  However, most GABA A  receptors are composed of two α subunits, two β subunits, and one γ subunit. 235  Different subunit types have different effects. For instance, the α 1  subunit of the GABA A  receptor is associated with sedation and hypnosis, 237  the α 2  and α 3  subunits are associated with antianxiety effects and muscle relaxation, 238  and the α 5  subunits are associated with pain relief and learning processes. 238  The GABA B  receptor is also involved in the regulation of neural networks 239  and has an important role in the pathogenesis of epilepsy, anxiety and depression. 240  In addition to its role as a neurotransmitter in the central nervous system, GABA also plays a significant role in metabolism. 241  The administration of GABA can ameliorate glucose tolerance in rodent models of type 2 diabetes, 242  reduce insulin resistance, 243  and decrease the risk of insulin resistance in their offspring. 244 Additionally, neurotensin (NTS), 66 , 79  neuropeptide S (NPS), 245  adenosine, and melatonin (which are discussed in detail below) also have significant impacts on the regulation of the sleep-wake cycle. In addition, studies on individuals with familial natural short sleep (FNSS) have identified mutations in the GRM1 gene 246  or the NPSR1 gene. 247  The former encodes metabotropic glutamate receptor 1, while the latter encodes neuropeptide S receptor 1. These mutations are associated with reduced total sleep time, while learning and memory abilities remain unaffected. 246 , 247 The synthesis, storage, and release of neurotransmitters and neuropeptides require a large amount of energy, 248  which is mainly derived from ATP produced by mitochondria. 249  Dynamic mitochondria within neurons can be transported to the axonal region to meet high metabolic demands. 250  In addition, mitochondrial depolarization in astrocytes also impacts neurotransmitter homeostasis. 251  Thus, energy metabolism serves as a fundamental determinant in maintaining physiological neurotransmitter dynamics. Energy metabolism affects the regulation of the sleep-wake cycle The two-process model 13  of sleep regulation is a key theoretical framework in sleep research that explains the regulatory mechanisms underlying the sleep-wake cycle. This model postulates that the balance between sleep and wakefulness is governed by two interrelated yet distinct physiological processes: Process S (the homeostatic sleep process) and Process C (the circadian process). Process S represents an intrinsic sleep-drive mechanism whose intensity increases proportionally with the duration of prior wakefulness. It is characterized by the accumulation of sleep pressure during extended wake periods and its subsequent dissipation during sleep, reflecting a dynamic “use-dependent” recovery system. Process C, primarily regulated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, also known as the central circadian pacemaker, is synchronized with the 24-hour earth rotation cycle. This process establishes a stable temporal framework for sleep-wake patterning, thereby preventing sleep from occurring at inappropriate times, such as during the day, and avoiding sustained wakefulness at night. Energy metabolism in the homeostasis of the sleep-wake cycle Sleep-wake homeostasis reflects the balance between sleep and wakefulness, involving the accumulation and release of sleep pressure. As the duration of wakefulness extends, sleep pressure gradually increases, leading to sleep debt. To adjust the state of sleep debt, the organism actively enters sleep. After undergoing sleep deprivation, subsequent sleep is often deeper or longer to compensate for missed sleep. During the transition between wakefulness and sleep, there are significant changes in brain energy metabolic activities and endogenous sleep-wake related substances. Previous studies have suggested that endogenous sleep-related substances, such as adenosine, mediate the increase in sleep pressure during wakefulness. Recent reports have found that the phosphorylation of some proteins is also involved in this process. 252 , 253 Adenosine signaling couples energy metabolism with the sleep-wake cycle Adenosine, formed by the hydrolysis of adenosine monophosphate (AMP) or S-adenosylhomocysteine, 254  is widely recognized as an endogenous sleep regulator. Injecting adenosine into the brains of animals can induce sleep behavior , 255  and different adenosine analogs dose-dependently increase the duration of NREM and REM sleep. 256  The extracellular adenosine levels in the BF of cats tend to rise during wakefulness and decline during sleep, with a particularly noticeable increase after prolonged wakefulness. 257  Selective activation of astrocytes or neurons in the NAc can remarkably increase extracellular adenosine levels and induce slow-wave sleep. 74  Therefore, adenosine can be considered a regulator reflecting sleep pressure. Additionally, adenosine can integrate light and sleep signals to regulate the circadian rhythms of mice. 258 Due to the lack of a visual detection method for adenosine in the past, the exact source of extracellular adenosine remained controversial. Recently, employing a newly optimized extracellular adenosine fluorescent probe based on the G protein-coupled receptor activation principle (GRAB-Ado), neurons have been revealed as the primary source of extracellular adenosine in the hippocampus. 259  Nucleoside homeostasis in humans is regulated by two protein families: the SLC28 family of Na + -coupled concentrative nucleoside transporters (CNTs) and the SLC29 family of equilibrative nucleoside transporters (ENTs). 260  ENTs passively transport adenosine across the cell membrane in both directions according to the concentration gradient. Under normal physiological conditions in the brain, the intracellular adenosine concentration in neurons is generally higher than the extracellular concentration via the pivotal roles of CNTs in maintaining intracellular adenosine levels by mediating its uptake from the extracellular space. 261  Hippocampal neuronal adenosine release is largely dependent on the coordinated action of concentrative nucleoside transporters (CNTs) and equilibrative nucleoside transporters (ENTs), which mediate intracellular-to-extracellular transport driven by a concentration gradient. This pathway significantly surpasses the contribution from vesicular release and ATP degradation via CD39/CD73. 259  During hypoxia, local potassium infusion, and ischemia, the extracellular adenosine concentration increases, 262  which is likely mediated by increasing the intracellular adenosine concentration or/and decreasing the activity of CNTs. Furthermore, using fiber-optic recording methods, Peng et al. 263  discovered that Ca 2+  activity in BF astrocytes and the levels of extracellular ATP change during the sleep-wake cycle. Additionally, these changes are related to the Ca 2+  activity of local glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons. The Ca 2+  activity of BF astrocytes and extracellular ATP levels are higher during wakefulness and REM sleep, and both are lower during NREM sleep. 263  The trend in extracellular adenosine levels is similar, but the extracellular ATP levels significantly decrease after inhibiting the Ca 2+  activity of BF astrocytes, while the extracellular adenosine levels show no significant change. 263  Moreover, in CD73 (a key enzyme involved in the hydrolysis of extracellular ATP to adenosine) knockout mice, the extracellular adenosine levels in the BF region are not different from those in normal mice. 263  These results all suggest that the increase in BF extracellular adenosine during waking and REM is mainly caused by ATP metabolism in neurons instead of extracellular ATP hydrolysis (Fig.  4a ). The interaction between sleep homeostasis and the circadian rhythm Sleep homeostasis (Process S) and the circadian rhythm (Process C) do not operate independently; instead, they function in a coordinated manner to collectively and precisely regulate sleep timing (when to sleep and how long to sleep), architecture, and quality. This synergistic interaction constitutes the classical two-process model, which serves as the cornerstone for understanding the stability and flexibility of the sleep-wake cycle. As the “command center”, Process C sets critical time windows for the accumulation and release of Process S; from another perspective, Process S acts as a “feedback signal”, which can calibrate and fine-tune the precision and intensity of Process C. First, by setting the rhythmic fluctuations of the “wake drive”, Process C defines the time window in which Process S can be expressed. The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), the core pacemaker of Process C, acts as a precise biological clock, whose primary function is to ensure the synchronization of bodily activities with the light-dark cycle of the external environment. During the light or active phase, the SCN activates wake-promoting brain areas such as the LC 342  and TMN, 343  enhancing the wake drive. This strong wake-promoting pressure can effectively suppress the sleep need accumulated by Process S, enabling individuals to maintain high alertness and activity capacity even after hours of wakefulness. In contrast, during the dark or rest phase, the activity pattern of the SCN undergoes a shift. By activating sleep-promoting centers such as the VLPO, it indirectly inhibits the activity of the aforementioned wake-promoting brain regions. 344  At this point, the wake drive is significantly weakened, clearing the way for the release of sleep needs. Therefore, Process S pressure, which has accumulated to a high level, can rapidly trigger sleep onset and effectively maintain the stability of the sleep state, preventing mid-sleep awakenings. This mechanism ensures that sleep is scheduled during specific time periods when energy consumption is at its lowest and the risk of predation is potentially highest, thereby holding significant adaptive and evolutionary importance. While Process S does not passively accept the regulation of Process C, it also calibrates the amplitude and stability of Process C crucially through neurochemical feedback. This process reflects the fine-tuning effect of the homeostatic mechanism on the biological clock. When sleep deprivation or insufficient sleep occurs, the sleep pressure of Process S continues to increase, and one of its core physiological indicators is the accumulation of endogenous sleep substances (such as adenosine) in the brain.
