Energy metabolic disorders predispose individuals to sleep disorders Sleep disorders constitute a clinical syndrome characterized by abnormal sleep quality, abnormal sleep duration, or disruptions in the sleep-wake rhythm, accompanied by impaired daytime functioning (such as fatigue, daytime sleepiness, and mood disturbances). According to the International Classification of Sleep Disorders (ICSD-3), sleep disorders can be divided into seven major categories, including insomnia disorders, sleep-related breathing disorders (SRBD), central disorders of hypersomnolence, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders, sleep-related movement disorders, parasomnias, and other sleep disorders. 368  Clinical evidence reveals a strong association between energy metabolism dysregulation and sleep disorders. A markedly elevated prevalence of sleep disorders is observed across populations with energy-metabolic disorders. This is particularly evident in the high burden of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), which affects up to 50–60% of obese individuals, 369  and the approximately 40% increase in insomnia symptoms observed among type 2 diabetes (T2DM) cohorts. 370  Similarly, conditions characterized by cellular energy deficit, including mitochondrial diseases, neurodegenerative disorders, and aging, show a 2-4-fold higher rate of insomnia, circadian misalignment, and REM-sleep behavior disorder. 371 Fatigue and excessive daytime sleepiness Fatigue and excessive daytime sleepiness are core, clinically significant symptoms of virtually all sleep disorders. They are also the primary reasons for patients to seek medical evaluation due to their profound impact on daily functioning, including impaired cognitive performance, reduced work productivity, and increased risk of accidents. To understand why these symptoms emerge, it is critical to first delineate the multifaceted functions of sleep. The key functions of sleep encompass the restoration of energy, 372  repair of physiological processes, 373  and regulation of metabolism and neuroendocrine functions. 3  When sleep disorders impair either the quality of sleep or its quantity, the body and brain are unable to complete essential restorative processes and energy replenishment. This failure directly leads to the manifestation of fatigue 374  or excessive daytime sleepiness, 375  both of which represent fundamental compensatory responses to an unmet sleep need. Fatigue, more precisely defined, is characterized as a pervasive, subjective sense of exhaustion, weariness, or a profound depletion of energy that is not relieved by rest. It is a highly prevalent symptom associated with nearly all types of sleep disorders. 376  In fact, epidemiological and clinical studies suggest that fatigue may be an even more ubiquitous complaint than self-reported sleepiness in many conditions, particularly those involving chronic sleep fragmentation or circadian rhythm disruptions, such as insomnia or shift work disorder. 377  The neurobiological underpinnings of fatigue are complex and multifactorial. Sleep disruption is known to dysregulate the hypothalamic‒pituitary‒adrenal (HPA) axis, leading to aberrant cortisol rhythms and altering the release of proinflammatory cytokines. 378  This combination of neuroendocrine dysfunction and low-grade systemic inflammation is thought to directly contribute to the sensation of bodily exhaustion and lack of energy. 379  Furthermore, disrupted sleep impairs cerebral energy metabolism and synaptic homeostasis in prefrontal cortical regions, which are critical for executive function and motivation. This central deficit can manifest subjectively as mental fatigue, characterized by difficulties with concentration, memory, and goal-directed behavior. 380 In contrast, excessive daytime sleepiness is a more specific symptom featured by an overwhelming, irresistible urge to fall asleep during intended wakefulness. It reflects a pathological state of an abnormally enhanced sleep drive within the sleep-wake balance. 381  It is not merely simple tiredness but rather signifies an impairment in the brain’s ability to maintain wakefulness. The neural basis for sleepiness lies in the dysfunction of ascending arousal systems. Excessive daytime sleepiness is most prominently and specifically observed in sleep disorders that cause one of two primary deficits: either a severe deterioration of nighttime sleep quality that leads to an uncompensated increase in homeostatic sleep pressure or a direct impairment of the wake-promoting neural circuits themselves. 382  The first mechanism is typified by disorders such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), where recurrent apneas cause continuous sleep fragmentation, preventing the natural progression into deep, restorative slow-wave sleep. 383  Despite adequate time in bed, sleep is nonrestorative, resulting in an immense sleep debt that manifests as severe sleepiness the following day. The second mechanism is evident in disorders of central origin, such as narcolepsy, where the fundamental pathology involves a loss of hypocretin/orexin-producing neurons in the hypothalamus. 384  These neurons are pivotal for stabilizing the switch between sleep and wake states. Their deficiency leads to an inherent instability of wakefulness, resulting in intrusive sleep episodes and persistent sleepiness, independent of the prior night’s sleep quality. This distinction is crucial for understanding the phenomenology of different sleep disorders. Energy metabolic disorders and sleep disorders Sleep disorders represent a significant and frequently overlooked comorbidity in individuals with energy metabolic disorders, such as T2DM and obesity. The relationship, however, extends far beyond mere coincidence. It is increasingly recognized as a complex, bidirectional interplay where each pathophysiological process exacerbates the other. Crucially, the brain regions that masterfully regulate sleep-wake cycles, particularly the SCN and hypothalamic circuits, are also central players in the control of energy balance, glucose homeostasis, and endocrine function. 385  Consequently, a sleep disruption that impacts duration, timing, or architecture can profoundly dysregulate metabolic pathways. Conversely, the state of cellular energy surplus and insulin resistance characteristic of T2DM and obesity can impair the normal function of these very same brain centers, thereby disrupting sleep. T2DM and sleep disorders The relationship between T2DM and sleep disorders is paradigmatic of a vicious, bidirectional cycle. Individuals with T2DM exhibit a markedly high prevalence of sleep problems (50–70%), most notably insomnia and restless legs syndrome during sleep, both of which are significantly associated with poorer glycemic control and reduced quality of life. 386 – 389  T2DM is characterized by abnormal insulin secretion. Insulin not only regulates peripheral blood glucose but also acts as a neuropeptide that promotes the release of GABA in the central nervous system, thereby reducing neuronal excitability. 390  During insulin resistance or insufficient insulin secretion, impaired central insulin signaling leads to attenuated GABAergic neurotransmission. This diminishes the capacity of the central nervous system to promote and maintain sleep drive, consequently resulting in hyperarousal. In addition, hyperglycemia per se can lead to both shorter sleep duration and worse sleep efficiency, 391  while nocturnal polyuria driven by osmotic diuresis also forces repeated awakenings and reduces sleep efficiency. Concurrent neuropathic pain further prolongs sleep latency and disrupts deep sleep stages, creating a vicious cycle of pain and sleep disturbance. 392  Conversely, the resulting sleep deprivation and fragmentation exert profound detrimental effects on glycemic control. Studies robustly show that insufficient sleep acutely induces peripheral insulin resistance. 393  In normal-weight healthy men, a single night of sleep deprivation can increase ghrelin levels and feelings of hunger. 394  These changes collectively exacerbate the core metabolic defects of T2DM. Furthermore, circadian misalignment, common in modern society, can directly impair pancreatic beta-cell function and insulin secretion, creating a storm for dysglycemia. 395  Therefore, in T2DM, sleep disorders are not merely a symptom but a critical contributor to disease progression, making sleep a novel therapeutic target for improving metabolic outcomes. Obesity and sleep disorders Obesity and sleep disorders are inextricably linked, with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) representing the most prominent and mechanistically direct connection. The pathophysiology is straightforward yet impactful: excessive adipose tissue, particularly in the neck and upper airway, leads to mechanical obstruction during sleep, causing recurrent apneas and hypopneas. 396  Nevertheless, 30–40% of OSA patients are not obese, highlighting that nonanatomical factors, such as low arousal threshold, poor upper-airway muscle responsiveness, and ventilatory control instability, also play significant roles. 397  These events result in chronic intermittent hypoxia, sleep fragmentation, and exaggerated sympathetic nervous system activation. Leptin, an adipocyte-derived hormone, promotes sleep by signaling energy sufficiency to the brain, thereby reducing metabolic activity and facilitating sleep initiation and maintenance. Conversely, ghrelin, primarily secreted from the stomach, enhances wakefulness and shortens sleep duration by stimulating appetite and increasing energy expenditure, signaling a state of energy need. 398  In states of aberrant lipid metabolism, such as obesity, the secretion of leptin and ghrelin becomes severely dysregulated. 399  Leptin resistance combined with relative ghrelin excess can directly perturb sleep-wake homeostasis, resulting in a state of hyperarousal. 400 , 401  Sleep reduction, even in the absence of frank OSA, is a significant risk factor for weight gain and obesity. Short sleep duration decreases leptin and increases ghrelin, leading to greater hunger and a preference for energy-dense foods. 402  This creates a powerful feedback loop: obesity promotes sleep disorders (such as OSA), which in turn aggravate metabolic dysfunction and promote further weight gain, making weight management exceptionally challenging. Energy deficiency and sleep disorders Unlike disorders of energy metabolism, energy-deficient conditions such as mitochondrial diseases, neurodegenerative diseases, and aging share a core pathophysiological feature: impaired ability to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the universal currency of energy. This intrinsic energy crisis directly impacts the highly metabolically active processes underlying both sleep homeostasis and circadian rhythmicity. Studies have found that in conditions of brain energy deficiency, such as primary mitochondrial diseases, neurodegenerative diseases (such as Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease), and aging, the incidence of sleep disorders is higher than that in the general population. 403 – 406 Primary mitochondrial diseases and sleep disorders Primary mitochondrial diseases are caused by genetic or spontaneous mutations in nuclear DNA or mitochondrial DNA, with defects in oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) being the primary characteristic. 407  The resultant failure in efficient energy generation creates a critical energy deficit that is particularly detrimental to highly metabolically active tissues. Neurons and muscle cells, with their exceptionally high energy demands for maintaining electrochemical gradients and contractile function, are disproportionately affected. Consequently, mitochondrial diseases typically manifest as progressive and multisystem disorders, with prominent neurological and neuromuscular degeneration being hallmark clinical features. 408  The high prevalence of sleep disorders in mitochondrial diseases is a direct consequence of cellular energy failure. Sleep-related breathing disorders are the primary type of sleep disturbance associated with mitochondrial diseases. Patients with severe skeletal muscle involvement often experience obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), while those with significant central nervous system involvement predominantly exhibit central sleep apnea (CSA). 409  Notably, the prevalence of these sleep-disordered breathing events is significantly higher in children with mitochondrial diseases than in the general pediatric population. This observation suggests that sleep-related breathing disturbances may serve as an early and sensitive clinical indicator of disease progression, often appearing before other overt neurological symptoms, thereby demonstrating the importance of routine polysomnographic screening in this vulnerable group. 410 Neurodegenerative diseases and sleep disorders The brain requires ATP produced from glucose metabolism as a continuous energy supply to maintain normal physiological states, with over 90% of brain ATP generated through OXPHOS. 411  In neurodegenerative diseases, brain glucose metabolism deteriorates in a progressive, region specific, and disease-specific manner, ultimately leading to insufficient energy supply to the brain. 323 , 412 , 413  Concurrent with this energy failure, clinical studies consistently report a remarkably high incidence of sleep disorders in patients with neurodegenerative conditions. 404 , 414 , 415  This co-occurrence is not coincidental but is underpinned by a critical bidirectional relationship. On the one hand, the brain’s energy deficit directly impairs the function of nuclei regulating sleep-wake cycles. On the other hand, sleep disorders amplify the underlying pathology. It is during slow-wave sleep that cerebrospinal fluid flow increases significantly, facilitating the clearance of metabolic waste products, including amyloid-beta and tau proteins. 357  Consequently, chronic sleep disorders can compromise this essential cleansing process, leading to the accumulation of neurotoxic aggregates and thereby accelerating neurodegeneration. Nevertheless, the manifestations of sleep disorders linked to various neurodegenerative conditions differ, potentially due to the distinct brain regions impacted by these diseases (Table  3 ). Table 3 The categories of sleep disorders that occur in association with energy metabolism-related diseases and the involvement sites Energy metabolism-related diseases Prevalence of Sleep Disorders Categories of Sleep Disorders Involvement Site References Type 2 diabetes 50–70% 390 Insomnia GABA release, hyperglycemia 391 , 453 RLS Peripheral neuropathy 389 Obesity 50–60% 372 OSA Neck fat accumulation 396 Primary mitochondrial diseases 47.6% 452 OSA CSA Skeletal muscle Neurons 409 Alzheimer’s Disease up to 45% 421 , 422 Not mentioned GABA signing 422 Not mentioned Tau protein 423 CRSWD IDO/SCN 323 , 424 , 425 Parkinson’s disease up to 98% 434 Insomnia Basal ganglia 433 RBD Posterior cortex 434 – 436 RLS Posterior cingulate cortex 437 CRSWD Melatonin 438 Aging 49.1% 454 CRSWD SCN 442 , 443 Insomnia: sleep fragmentation Hcrt/OX neurons 444 – 446 , 448 Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder, with the most notable clinical manifestation being the progressive loss of cognitive function. AD is characterized by a profound cerebral energy deficit stemming from reduced glucose uptake, a dampened tricarboxylic acid cycle, and mitochondrial dysfunction, which collectively compromise the metabolic support provided by astrocytes and oligodendrocytes to neurons. 413 , 416  Sleep disturbances are common complications in AD patients, and epidemiological studies have reported that up to 45% of AD patients have sleep disorders. 417 – 420  Sleep disorders are present from the early stages of AD and tend to intensify as the disease progresses. 421  In AD patients, the expression of GABA signaling in the temporal lobe cortex is reduced, indicating an imbalance in the excitation/inhibition ratio in this region. 422  During the progression of AD, the deposition of amyloid-beta (Aβ) and tau proteins occurs. Among these, the tau protein can promote the degeneration of sleep-wake-related neurons, thereby affecting sleep. 423  Aβ and tau can also activate IDO in astrocytes, increasing the kynurenine metabolic pathway of tryptophan and leading to a decrease in the production of melatonin generated from tryptophan via serotonin. 323  In 1985, Swaab, Fliers, and Partiman found that the volume and number of cells in the SCN of AD patients are significantly reduced. 424  Compared to wild-type mice, the A-type potassium current on SCN neurons in the AD mouse model is notably weakened, suggesting the presence of neurophysiological damage in the SCN in AD. 425  The impairment of the SCN partly explains the frequent occurrence of circadian rhythm disorders in AD patients. Furthermore, in the 5×FAD mouse model, a reduction in vascular density and decreased blood flow velocity were also observed in the retrosplenial cortex (RSC), 426  indicating that this region is in a state of hypometabolism. Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a chronic, progressive neurodegenerative disorder that manifests through a complex cluster of both motor and nonmotor symptoms. Among these, sleep disturbances are the most common nonmotor symptoms of PD, encompassing all forms of sleep disorders. 427 – 429  The pervasiveness of this issue is starkly highlighted by a comprehensive questionnaire survey, which revealed that up to 98% of PD patients had experienced it. One symptom has led to significant nighttime sleep problems since disease onset. 430  The primary pathological signature of PD is the selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) of the midbrain. Critically, this neuronal degeneration is accompanied by significant mitochondrial fragmentation and dysfunction within this vulnerable region, characterized by impairments in key energy-producing pathways such as reduced glycolysis and a marked decrease in the activity of mitochondrial complex I. 431 , 432  As previously mentioned, dopaminergic neurons contribute to the regulation of wakefulness and REM sleep and interact intricately with an array of neurotransmitters and neural circuits. 147  The degeneration of these circuits triggers a wide spectrum of specific sleep pathologies. Therefore, PD patients may experience sleep problems such as insomnia, 433  RBD, 434 – 436  restless leg syndrome (RLS), 437  and CRSWD. 438 Aging and sleep disorders Broadly speaking, aging is defined as the time-related functional decline that affects most organisms, characterized by the gradual loss of physiological integrity. As cells and organisms age, the efficiency of the respiratory chain tends to decline, leading to increased electron leakage and reduced ATP production. 439 – 441  In mammals, advancing age is associated with a progressive deterioration of the SCN, 442  which can lead to a diminished amplitude of circadian rhythms, reduced rhythmicity, decreased sensitivity to light exposure, and an intensification of the sleep pattern characterized by going to bed and rising earlier than usual. 443  Meanwhile, the sleep structure of older adults undergoes a series of noticeable changes, such as prolonged sleep latency, reduced overall sleep time, increased sleep fragmentation, and decreased deep sleep. 444 – 446  In addition to the overall changes in sleep structure, the sleep characteristic oscillations measured by EEG also change, most notably the reduction of two-component oscillations related to NREM sleep: slow waves and sleep spindles. 447  Lecea and colleagues found that the expression of KCNQ2/3 channels on hypocretin/orexin neurons in the hypothalamus of aged mice was reduced compared to that in younger mice, making wakefulness-promoting Hcrt/orexin neurons more excitable, thereby leading to a disruption of the sleep-wake cycle. 448 Medications that optimize energy metabolism can improve sleep Energy metabolism serves as the fundamental basis of all life activities and is intricately involved in numerous physiological processes. These include maintaining neurotransmitter homeostasis, facilitating protein phosphorylation, and generating endogenous sleep-promoting substances such as adenosine and melatonin. Collectively, these functions underscore that energy metabolism is closely linked to sleep regulation. Therefore, enhancing energy metabolism may be a promising therapeutic strategy for sleep disorders. Several metabolism-modifying agents have now been identified to exert considerable sleep-promoting effects (Table  4 ). This metabolism-targeted intervention strategy offers a novel therapeutic direction beyond traditional sedative-hypnotic drugs, demonstrating particular potential for treating sleep disorders accompanied by metabolic dysregulation. Table 4 Some medications that enhance energy metabolism can improve sleep Drugs categories Impact on energy metabolism Impact on sleep Reference Biguanides Improve glucose metabolism and mitochondrial function Increase sleep duration and sleep efficiency 455 – 457 GLP-1 receptor agonists Improve glucose metabolism and lipid metabolism Play a crucial role in the management of OSA 461 , 462 Melatonin and melatonin receptor agonists Reduce triglycerides and total cholesterol levels, while increase glycemic variability Regulate the circadian rhythm 463 – 465 Orexin receptor antagonists and agonists Orexin receptor antagonists Reduce appetite and inhibit feeding behavior Improve sleep onset and sleep maintenance endpoints 472 – 474 Orexin receptor agonists Increase appetite and promote feeding behavior Enhance wakefulness, reduce daytime sleepiness, and alleviate cataplexy 478 Nicotinamide mononucleotide Boost insulin sensitivity and muscle function Ameliorate sleep quality 480 – 484 Biguanides Metformin, the first-line pharmacological agent for managing type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), has gained increasing attention not only for its core role in glycemic control but also for its broader beneficial effects. Multiple studies have demonstrated that it can significantly improve metabolic profiles, safeguard mitochondrial function, and potentially decelerate the aging process while extending lifespan. 449 , 450  It is well established that type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and sleep disorders exhibit a bidirectional relationship. 451  On the one hand, the presence of sleep disturbances can exert adverse effects on metabolic homeostasis: they disrupt the balance of appetite-regulating hormones and impair insulin sensitivity, thereby increasing the risk of developing T2DM over time. 452  On the other hand, T2DM can itself impair the initiation and maintenance of sleep through multiple pathways, including compromised central insulin signaling leading to reduced GABA synthesis 390 , 453  and nocturnal glucose fluctuations resulting in sympathetic nervous system excitation. 454  Given this bidirectional link, metformin’s efficacy in improving insulin sensitivity and glycemic control may thereby contribute to improved sleep outcomes. A retrospective observational study indicated that individuals with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin exhibit longer sleep duration and better sleep efficiency than those not on metformin. 455  Moreover, this sleep-benefiting effect of metformin is not limited to T2DM patients. Studies conducted in patients with metabolic syndrome 456  and polycystic ovary syndrome during adolescence 457  have also confirmed that metformin treatment increases sleep duration and sleep efficiency, highlighting its potential as a multifaceted agent for addressing metabolic and sleep-related comorbidities. GLP-1 receptor agonists GLP-1 receptor agonists have emerged as highly effective therapeutic agents for metabolic disorders, as they improve both glucose metabolism and lipid metabolism disorders, demonstrating excellent effects in lowering blood sugar and promoting weight loss. 458 , 459  The accumulation of neck fat due to obesity serves as the primary pathological basis for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). 460  This extra fat in the neck area presses on the upper airway. When this happens, the airway collapses repeatedly during sleep, disrupting breathing and causing periods of low oxygen. GLP-1 receptor agonists help with this root issue because they lead to significant weight loss. They do this by suppressing appetite and promoting energy expenditure and therefore play a crucial role in the management of OSA. 461  In the phase III SURMOUNT-OSA trial ( NCT05412004 ) of tirzepatide, 52 weeks of treatment reduced the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) from a baseline of 35.8 events per hour to 8.4 events per hour in patients with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), representing a 76.5% reduction. 462  Additionally, 42.2% to 50.2% of patients achieved disease remission, defined as an AHI < 5 events per hour or an Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) score ≤10 462 . Based on these findings, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved tirzepatide as the first medication for the treatment of moderate-to-severe OSA in patients with obesity. Melatonin and melatonin receptor agonists Melatonin is commonly considered a chronobiotic agent and is mainly used for patients with circadian rhythm disorders. 463  Beyond its role in regulating circadian rhythms, randomized controlled trials have shed light on other effects of melatonin supplementation. These studies show that it can significantly reduce triglycerides and total cholesterol levels 464  but increases glycemic variability in patients with type 2 diabetes. 465  Compared to other hypnotic drugs, melatonin produces fewer side effects but also has a lesser degree of improvement in sleep. 463  Melatonin has a short half-life, approximately 20–50 min, which makes it difficult to maintain therapeutic effects throughout the night, limiting its use in patients with difficulty maintaining sleep. 466  To address this weakness, Circadin, a sustained-release formulation of melatonin, has been developed. This type of medication gradually releases melatonin over several hours, mimicking the secretion pattern during the night. 467  Currently, two melatonin receptor agonists have been approved for the treatment of sleep disorders: ramelteon and tasimelteon. They both have agonistic effects on MT 1  and MT 2  receptors. In addition, tasimelteon is the only drug approved by the FDA for the treatment of non-24-h sleep-wake disorder, a circadian rhythm disorder affecting blind individuals. 466 , 468  Notably, similar to melatonin, the impact of melatonin sustained-release formulations and melatonin receptor agonists on overall sleep time appears to be limited. 467 , 469 Orexin receptor antagonists and agonists Orexin (also known as hypocretin) is a neuropeptide produced in the hypothalamus that plays two primary physiological roles: regulating the sleep-wake cycle and modulating energy metabolism and appetite. Dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs) are a novel class of hypnotic drugs that have emerged in recent years. Suvorexant, Lemborexant, and Daridorexant were approved by the FDA in 2014, 2019, and 2022, respectively. 470  Compared to traditional hypnotics, DORAs have fewer side effects and can maintain a more natural sleep architecture. 470 , 471  Clinical trials have shown that DORAs are clinically useful in improving both sleep onset and sleep maintenance endpoints. 472 – 474  Orexin has already become deficient in narcolepsy, 384  so DORAs are contraindicated for these patients. Although cases of sleep paralysis and muscle weakness have been observed in clinical trials, there is no evidence to suggest that treatment with DORAs increases the incidence of cataplexy. 473 – 475  However, the use of DORAs may affect driving ability, suggesting that DORAs can impair the ability to maintain alertness and attention. 476 , 477  Type 1 narcolepsy is a hypersomnolence disorder resulting from the degeneration of orexin-producing neurons, leading to deficient orexin signaling in the central nervous system. Treatment with oveporexton, an orexin receptor 2-selective agonist, has been shown to enhance wakefulness, reduce daytime sleepiness, and alleviate cataplexy in affected individuals. 478 Nicotinamide mononucleotide NMN is a key precursor molecule for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), an essential coenzyme in the human body. NAD +  participates in a wide range of vital physiological processes. It is deeply involved in cellular metabolism, 446  DNA repair, and mitochondrial maintenance. 479  As people age, their body’s NAD+ levels usually start to drop. This decline is linked to a variety of health issues, from reduced cellular function to increased risk of age-related conditions. However, research has shown that supplementation with NMN can help reverse this trend by boosting NAD+ levels in the body. For middle-aged and senior adults, NMN supplementation has been found to improve insulin sensitivity, which helps regulate blood sugar more effectively. 480  It also enhances muscle function in healthy older men, supporting mobility and strength. 481  Additionally, there is evidence suggesting that it may slow the aging process and even extend life expectancy. Importantly, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trials have provided further proof of NMN’s benefits. These trials show that taking NMN supplements can improve sleep quality, with positive effects seen in both people with chronic insomnia and elderly individuals. 482 – 484 Conclusion and future perspectives Sleep is a fundamental, universally observed phenomenon across the natural world, present in nearly all complex organisms from humans to many animals. Beyond its role as a period of rest, ensuring sufficient high-quality sleep is a critical factor in sustaining overall health and enhancing quality of life. It supports immune function, cognitive performance, emotional regulation, and metabolic balance, all of which are essential for long-term well-being. Sleep is not an isolated process and is closely linked to a wide range of factors. Environmental elements such as noise, light exposure, and temperature can disrupt sleep cycles. Mental and psychological states, such as stress, anxiety, or depression, often interfere with falling or staying asleep. Demographic factors such as gender and age also significantly affect sleep, with women and older adults being more susceptible to insomnia and declining sleep quality, respectively. Additionally, lifestyle behaviors such as irregular sleep schedules, excessive caffeine intake, or lack of physical activity, as well as genetic predispositions to certain sleep disorders, all contribute to shaping an individual’s sleep health. Given the complexity of factors influencing sleep, it is clear that a one-size-fits-all approach is insufficient for treating sleep disorders. Instead, we should develop comprehensive and personalized therapeutic strategies tailored to each patient’s unique circumstances. This is especially important when managing sleep disorders in patients who also have disturbances in glucose or lipid metabolism. For example, patients with insulin resistance or T2DM often struggle with sleep, and poor sleep can further worsen their glycemic control. Similarly, those with hyperlipidemia or obesity face higher risks of obstructive sleep apnea, a condition that in turn exacerbates metabolic issues. In these cases, treatment must address both the sleep disorder and the underlying metabolic problems simultaneously. When selecting medications for sleep disorders, careful consideration of potential side effects is crucial, especially in patients with comorbid metabolic conditions. While drugs such as olanzapine and quetiapine are sometimes used off-label to treat insomnia, particularly in patients who also have anxiety, depression, or other psychiatric disorders, their metabolic adverse effects are well documented. These effects include weight gain, increased insulin resistance, and elevated lipid levels, all of which can worsen existing glucose or lipid metabolism disorders. 485 , 486  For this reason, these agents should be avoided as much as possible in patients with coexisting metabolic issues. Another important connection to consider is the link between sleep disorders, mitochondrial function, and age-related or degenerative diseases. As previously noted, conditions such as mitochondrial diseases, neurodegenerative disorders (such as AD or PD), and even the natural aging process are often accompanied by mitochondrial dysfunction and energy deficiency. Mitochondria function as the “powerhouses” of the cell, generating ATP to supply the primary energy required for cellular activities. When mitochondrial function declines, energy production drops, and this can disrupt the capability of the brain to regulate sleep-wake cycles. Sleep disorders frequently appear in the early stages of these conditions. As the disease progresses, these sleep problems often become more severe, creating a vicious cycle where poor sleep further impairs mitochondrial function and accelerates disease progression. This connection suggests that sleep disorders can serve as an early warning sign for these diseases. Early pharmacological intervention to enhance energy metabolism and improve sleep may help delay or prevent disease onset. Furthermore, in cases where sleep disorders already coexist with mitochondrial diseases, neurodegenerative diseases or age-related energy deficiency, clinicians should consider incorporating pharmacological agents that enhance mitochondrial function and energy metabolism into the sleep management plan. By targeting the underlying energy deficit, these agents can address the root cause of sleep disorders, leading to more effective and sustainable improvements in sleep quality and overall health. In summary, this review discusses the role of energy metabolism in sleep from multiple perspectives, including its involvement in supporting neural activity during sleep-wake cycles, maintaining circadian rhythm stability, and modulating the function of sleep regulating brain regions. It emphasizes that normal energy metabolism is not only essential for sustaining normal sleep but also a key prerequisite for preventing sleep disorders triggered by metabolic imbalances. Additionally, the review provides a novel therapeutic angle for treating sleep disorders by targeting and improving energy metabolism pathways, offering potential alternatives to conventional symptomatic treatments. However, there remains a notable gap in research regarding the specific molecular mechanisms underlying the interaction between energy metabolism and sleep, such as how mitochondrial function or metabolite signaling directly regulates the sleep-wake cycle. Thus, more in depth, mechanism-focused studies are urgently needed in the future to bridge this knowledge gap and guide the development of targeted interventions.
fulltext_by_pmid.23853635: INTRODUCTION Insomnia is a condition of unsatisfactory quantity and/or quality of sleep, which persists for a considerable period of time, including difficulty falling asleep, difficulty staying asleep, or early final wakening. Insomnia is not necessarily an inevitable consequence of aging, but its prevalence increases with age[ 1 2 ] and most elderly people who have not appropriate geriatric conditions, may suffer from major sleep disorders.[ 3 ] In other words, aging itself does not lead to sleep disorders, and this problem is due to other factors associated with aging.[ 4 ] The most important age-related sleep changes include decreased sleep duration, decreased sleep efficiency (SE) (the percentage of sleeping time after going to bed), and decreased short-wave sleep, which all are categorized as insomnia.[ 5 6 ] The prevalence of insomnia in all population groups is between 10% and 48%.[ 1 ] One population survey of insomnia prevalence in the elderly found that 42% of participants reported difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep. Following up, the results of the study for 3 years found that 15% of contributors who did not reported insomnia had disturbed sleep, suggesting an annual incidence rate of approximately 5 percent.[ 2 ] In other statistics, the insomnia is estimated to be present in 40-50% percent of elderly people above 60 years of age.[ 7 ] In all age groups, the individuals who suffer from insomnia show memory weakness, increased reaction time, short-term memory problems, and lowered efficacy level. However, insomnia is more problematic in elderly subjects, because it puts them at higher risk for falling, cognitive impairments, weak physical function, and mortality (from 1.3 to 3 times higher than normal subjects).[ 8 9 10 ] Sleep disorders are also related to decreased quality of life and general health and increased health costs, stress, and depression symptoms.[ 11 ] Currently, insomnia treatment includes medicinal and nonmedicinal treatments. Regarding the effects of nonmedicinal methods in insomniac individuals, there are low or medium quality evidences, or no important clinical results. In general, there is no precise information about the beneficial effects of these methods on insomnia treatment compared to control groups.[ 12 ] Medicinal treatment of insomnia is done through a broad spectrum of drugs; however, Sleep Disorders Conference of American National Institutes of Health has declared that drugs used routinely for treatment of sleep disorders have more hazards than benefits and are not recommended for elderly.[ 13 ] Particularly, there is a concern about elderly people, since 81% of hypnotic drugs are used in daily and long-term patterns by them.[ 14 ] Magnesium is the fourth most abundant cation in the body and the second most abundant intracellular cation. It is involved in more than 300 biochemical reactions of the body.[ 15 ] Magnesium is an essential cofactor for many enzymatic reactions, especially those that are involved in energy metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.[ 16 ] Aging is a major risk factor for magnesium deficiency. Numerous changes are occurring in magnesium status during elderly. Its total level reduces due to a decrease in bone mass which is the most important magnesium source in the body. Epidemiologic studies show that despite important physiologic role of magnesium, its dietary intake is inadequate in various societies,[ 17 18 19 20 ] and some population groups, especially elderly people have low magnesium intake,[ 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 ] which can be due to inability in using magnesium sources or their tendencies to consume more processed food and less whole grains and green leafy vegetables. However, it is shown that magnesium requirements do not change by aging.[ 25 ] Other alterations in magnesium metabolism, which are related to aging, are reduced magnesium intake, reduced intestinal uptake, increased urinal and fecal excretion, and drug induced.[ 16 26 ] Meanwhile, it seems that reduced magnesium intake has the most important role in age-related magnesium deficiency.[ 26 ] Dietary magnesium deficiency in the elderly is much higher than expected and its intake decreases continuously and exponentially with age, independent of gender and race.[ 21 ] NHANCES III analysis shows that elders’ magnesium intake in United States is much less than recommended dietary allowance (RDA) and compared to recommended levels of 420 and 320 mg/day, respectively for men and women, is equal to 225 mg/day for men and 166 mg/day for women. Yet, little is known about the magnesium status in Iran, especially in elderly population. The only well-designed population-based survey in Iran of dietary magnesium intake was conducted from 1999 through 2001 (within the framework of the Tehran Lipid and Glucose Study). A striking result of an analysis of that survey was the lower mean magnesium intake among participants. In aforementioned study, 95% of subjects failed to meet magnesium requirements (137 ± 28 mg/day).[ 27 ] Although the effect of magnesium on neural function and sleep behaviors is not fully understood, magnesium has an essential role in ion channels conductivity, such as  N -Methyl-D-aspartic acid (NMDA) receptor, and unilateral entrance of potassium channels. In addition, magnesium is essential for connection of monoamines to their receptors. Thus, this cation has a key role in neural transmission at cellular level, both in presynaptic membrane and postsynaptic membrane. Several studies have also acknowledged the role of magnesium in the regulation of central nervous system excitability.[ 28 ] Therefore, magnesium as a natural antagonist of NMDA and agonist of GABA seems to play a critical role in sleep regulation. According to mentioned issues, if magnesium supplementation can prevent insomnia side effects through its improvement, it can be used as an alternative treatment of routine drugs or in combination with them in order to reduce their numerous side effects. For this purpose, the present study is conducted to determine the impact of magnesium supplementation on insomnia in elderly. MATERIALS AND METHODS Subjects Based on evidences in the literature[ 29 30 31 32 ] and regarding to Held  et al . study,[ 31 ] concentration of serum renin was chosen to estimate the sample size. Serum renin concentration was expected to have 0.6 mIU/ml difference between placebo and supplementation groups. A sample size of 21 participants per group has 80% power to detect such a difference and a significance level of 5%. To adjust for an expected drop-out rate of 10%, approximately 46 participants (23 per group) needed to be enrolled in the study. So subjects consisted of 46 volunteers, (23 women, 23 men; age 65 ± 4.6) who entered the study after passing through psychiatric examinations and insomnia severity index (ISI) test, in order to confirm their primary insomnia (clinically moderate or severe), and their sleep time (ST) was registered in sleep log forms for 14 days, prior to begin supplementation (run-in phase). Investigators assigned consecutive code numbers to participants from a prespecified list. Simple sampling method was used to select patients who were then randomly allocated into the magnesium or the placebo group and received 500 mg elemental magnesium or placebo daily for 8 weeks. For those who were consistent with inclusion criteria and lacked the exclusion criteria of the study, the benefits, the aim, and duration of the study, and mode of intervention were described in a briefing. Criteria for inclusion in our double-blind randomized clinical trial included: Willing to cooperate, age 60-75 years, having insomnia according to ISI and sleep-log questionnaires, having body mass index (BMI) range of 25-34.9, dietary intake of magnesium under 75% RDA; serum magnesium level under 0.95 mmol/L, not receiving loop diuretics, cyclosporine, digoxin, amphotericin and any hormonal treatment, not having renal diseases, acute heart failure, sleep-related movement disorders (such as restless leg syndrome), and sleep-related respiratory disorders (such as sleep apnea). Reasons for exclusion from the study were: Psychiatric disorder history, recent stressful life events (e.g., divorce or death or acute illness of a family member), substance or alcohol abuse, and a transmeridian flight during last 6 weeks. Written informed consent was obtained from all subjects. The study was approved by ethics committee of Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences. Study design and measurements The study was performed in a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled parallel design, in January to March 2012 in Health Divisions of Cultural Centers of Tehran's 1, 10, and 14 districts. Magnesium was administered as magnesium oxide tablets twice a day (each tablet containing 414 mg magnesium oxide as 250 mg elemental magnesium) for 8 weeks. Questionnaires of ISI, physical activity, and sleep log were completed at baseline and after the intervention period. Anthropometric confounding factors, daily intake of magnesium, calcium, potassium, caffeine, calorie form carbohydrates, and total calorie intake, were obtained using 24-h recall for 3 days. To analyze biochemical factors of contributors, they were asked to be fasted for 12 h. Then venous blood samples were collected by a trained nurse and cooled rapidly to 2°C, then within 2-3 h, the blood samples were centrifuged with 3500 g velocity for 15 min and the sera were put in a −80°C freezer. The serum magnesium level was measured through atomic absorption spectrometry method and its cortisol, renin, and melatonin levels were measured through ELISA method. After collecting biochemical samples, anthropometric measurements were done by trained colleagues; so, according to WHO standards, the light cloth worn patients were weighted and their height were measured without shoes with a 0.5 cm accuracy wall meter. Using the weight (in kilograms) divided by height (in meters) square formula, BMI was calculated and the obtained information was recorded in general information questionnaire of patients. These measurements were repeated at the end of eighth week of the study. Statistical methods Quantitative variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. All variables were tested for normality by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test before any statistical comparisons were made, then if their distribution were normal in the population, to compare the quantitative variables and their mean in each group the paired  t -test, and to compare their mean between two groups, the independent samples  t -test were used. If the distribution was not normal, to compare within the groups, Wilcoxon test was used and to compare between the groups Mann-Whitney test was used. To compare the qualitative confounding variables between two groups, Chi-square test was used. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software version 19 and  P  values < 0.05 were considered as statistically significant. Also 0.05 <  P  values < 0.1 were reported as marginally significant. RESULTS Of 46 persons participating in the study, 2 persons due to not regular consumption of supplement or placebo and 1 person due to not participating in second turn blood sampling were excluded from the study. At the end, 43 persons (21 men and 22 women) completed the study. The age, weight, height, and BMI means and standard deviations of contributors were 65 ± 4.6 years (control: 65.4 ± 4.5; intervention: 64.7 ± 4.7), 72.1 ± 9.7 kg) control: 73.1 ± 9.5; intervention: 71 ± 10), 157 ± 8.1 cm (control: 156 ± 6.4; intervention: 158.5 ± 9.5), and 29.2 ± 3.7 kg/m 2 ) control: 30.11 ± 4.1; intervention: 28.23 ± 3.11), respectively. The dietary intakes of the study participants at the baseline and end of the study are shown in  table 1 . During the study, the dietary intake of individuals in none of investigated micronutrients and caffeine intake showed no significant statistical difference. In this study the changes of weight ( P  = 0.07) and BMI ( P  = 0.07) between two groups were not significant. Physical activity level ( P  = 0.02) in magnesium supplement group compared to placebo group showed a significant increase, which based on literature is presumed to be related to the fact that improvement in sleep patterns through decrement of daytime fatigue and sleepiness and their related high risk behaviors, results in increment of daily physical activity level.[ 33 34 35 ] Table 1 Means and standard deviations of dietary confounding factors in magnesium supplementation and placebo groups at baseline Table 2  summarizes sleep indices evaluations. As compared to the placebo group, in the experimental group, dietary magnesium supplementation brought about statistically significant increases in ST ( P  = 0.002) and SE ( P  = 0.03). Also sleep onset latency (SOL) ( P  = 0.02) and early morning awakening (EMA) ( P  = 0.08) decreased significantly and marginally significant, respectively. However, total sleep time (TST) ( P  = 0.37) did not show any significant differences between two groups. In addition, the obtained ISI ( P  = 0.006) from ISI questionnaire revealed a significant decrease between two groups, in statistical terms [ Table 2 ]. Table 2 Comparison of sleep indices in magnesium supplementation and placebo groups before and after intervention At the beginning of the study, no significant difference was seen in serum concentrations of investigated biochemical indices between two groups. The mean of changes of fasting magnesium, renin, cortisol, and melatonin levels were compared between two groups receiving magnesium supplement and placebo, via independent  t -test. As compared to the placebo group, in the experimental group, the serum renin ( P  < 0.001) and melatonin ( P  = 0.007) levels showed a significant increase and serum cortisol level ( P  = 0.008) showed a significant decrease [ Table 3 ]. Despite favorable increase of serum magnesium level during this study, the related changes in its level were just marginally significant ( P  = 0.06).  Table 4  also shows the effect of magnesium supplementation or placebo on percent change of subjective and objective measures of insomnia in control and experimental groups. Table 3 Comparing serum magnesium and biochemical indices of circadian cycle in magnesium supplementation and placebo groups before and after intervention Table 4 Percent change in subjective and objective measures of insomnia in participants, after 8 weeks of supplementation as compared with controls DISCUSSION This double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial is the first study to the knowledge of the authors, to survey the interdependent role of magnesium in treatment of insomnia and to show that magnesium supplementation results in significantly improvement of subjective and objective measures of insomnia than a placebo treatment in elderly people experiencing primary insomnia. The benefits of this supplementation in primary insomnia, in elderly subjects, appear to have significant clinical importance because insomnia is common in late life, which if left untreated may have clinical, economic, and human consequences for the individual and society.[ 25 36 ] Magnesium is an essential element that is crucial to hundreds of physiologic processes in humans. Not surprisingly, inadequate intake of magnesium has been linked to various adverse health outcomes, including sleep disorders. Despite the physiologic role of magnesium and its proven or potential benefits, epidemiologic surveys show that the dietary intake of magnesium is inadequate in various populations.[ 17 18 19 20 27 ] The findings of magnesium intake below recommendations by many raise the issue of the adequacy of magnesium status in population.[ 21 ] Yet, little is known about the magnesium status in Iran, especially in elderly population. The only well-designed population-based survey in Iran of dietary magnesium intake was conducted from 1999 through 2001 (within the framework of the Tehran Lipid and Glucose Study). A striking result of an analysis of that survey was the lower mean magnesium intake among participants. In aforementioned study, 95% of subjects failed to meet magnesium requirements (137 ± 28 mg/day).[ 27 ] Some population groups, such as the elderly, have particularly lower magnesium intake than reference groups[ 17 22 ] and aging is a major risk factor for magnesium deficiency. Dietary habits, nutrient intakes and aging processes are interrelated and are of particular importance among the elderly.[ 37 ] Numerous changes occurred in magnesium status during elderly. Its total level reduces due to a decrease in bone mass which is the most important magnesium source in the body. Also, lower magnesium intake may occur due to inability in using magnesium sources or their tendencies to consume more processed food and less whole grains and green leafy vegetables. Other alterations in magnesium metabolism, related to aging, are reduced intestinal uptake, increased urinal and fecal excretion, and drug induced.[ 16 26 ] Meanwhile, it seems that reduced magnesium intake has the most important role in age-related magnesium deficiency.[ 26 ] Nuts, seeds and beans, whole grains, and fish and seafood are the best sources of magnesium in the diet. In addition to the above foods, dark green leafy vegetables are good sources of magnesium.[ 37 ] Several studies have suggested that the effect of age on dietary habits may be attributable to functional impairments[ 38 39 ] and chewing problems.[ 40 41 ] Reduced functional capacity might have a large influence on food choice and, as a consequence, on nutrient intake — especially magnesium, regarding to its dietary sources — in old age. Older people chose different foods, suggesting that older persons tend to adapt their diet to the functional difficulties that often occur during the aging process. These factors may lead elderly persons to have a monotonous and energy-restricted diet, which easily results in an inadequate intake of nutrients.[ 42 ] There are a limited numbers of epidemiologic studies, of sufficient size that have assessed magnesium status in the elderly population, which makes it difficult to make specific recommendations on magnesium intakes in subgroups of older persons. But review of findings of previous studies suggests that treatment of potential physical and functional problems, increasing consumption of magnesium sources such as nuts, seeds and beans, whole grains and dark green leafy vegetables and increasing the dietary diversity — which is associated with diet quality—[ 37 ] within the context of a diet that maintains the appropriate energy balance and if required, magnesium supplementation, might be a good recommendation for this population to meet their requirements. The results of our study showed that ST ( P  = 0.002) and SE ( P  = 0.03) increased and SOL ( P  = 0.02) decreased, both significantly. However, TST ( P  = 0.37) and EMA ( P  = 0.08) did not show a significant difference. In addition, the obtained ISI ( P  = 0.006) from ISI questionnaire revealed a significant decrease. Results of the present study about the role of magnesium in sleep regulation are consistent with  Dralle  and  Bodeker  study, which showed that there is an association between magnesium supplementation and REM, muscle tone, and gross body movements in infants. Results of  Dralle  and  Bodeker  also suggested that there is a relationship between serum magnesium level and active sleep, likewise between serum magnesium level and quiet sleep. In their study magnesium supplementation increased the quiet sleep and decreased the active sleep.[ 29 ] Also, the results of our study are consistent with  Murck  and  Steiger  study in which the most important effects of Mg 2+  supplementation were an increment in spindle power during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and a change in delta power in the in the third sleep cycle.[ 30 ] In a study conducted by  Held et al . to analyze magnesium supplementation effects on sleep EEG, plasma ACTH, cortisol, AVP, renin, angiotensin II, and aldosterone in elderly, which showed that the most important Mg 2+  supplementation effect in healthy elderly subjects was short wave sleep (SWS) increment.[ 31 ] Also, the results of our study are consistent with  Rondanelli et al . study, which was done to investigate the effects of combined melatonin, magnesium, and zinc supplementation, which showed that the supplementation resulted in total score improvement of Pittsburg questionnaire compared to placebo, and suggested that treatment has beneficial effects on capability of recovering body activities through sleep.[ 32 ] In the present study, regarding to increase in SE — as the best total scale of insomnia[ 43 ] — from 0.63 to 0.73 in supplement group, it can be concluded that despite lack of change in TST of each person, if ST and adequacy of sleep increased and SOL decreased, in the same range, there is no need to increase TST in order to relieve the fatigue caused by daily activities and to recover body's ability through sleep. In the present study, serum magnesium level in supplement group tended to augment ( P  = 0.06); however, difference between two groups was just marginally significant at the end of the study. The method used for magnesium status assessment in the present study was the measurement of serum magnesium concentration. Since 99% of magnesium is in the bone and soft tissue, clinical assessment of magnesium status is difficult and has become now a challenge for clinical laboratories.[ 44 ] Based on the observations of several investigations, currently serum magnesium analysis appears to be the most practical, accessible, and expeditious method of identifying changes in magnesium homeostasis.[ 45 ] The obtained results from our study are consistent with the study of  Hoogerbrugge et al . who investigated the effect of supplementation with 1 gram magnesium oxide for 6 weeks on Lp(a) level in hypercholesterolemic patients and did not observe a significant difference in serum magnesium increment.[ 46 ]  Held et al . also, in a study which dealt with magnesium supplementation in 12 healthy persons, could not recognize a significant difference between two groups, despite detection of serum magnesium tendency toward increase in the supplementation group.[ 31 ] The study of  Rodriguez et al ., which dealt with magnesium supplementation in the treatment of depression in diabetic elderly subjects, reported a significant difference in serum magnesium level in supplement group compared to placebo group.[ 47 ]  Haddad et al . also, in their study, reported a significant increase in serum magnesium of the group which received intravenous magnesium compared to placebo group.[ 48 ] Guerrero and Rodriguez in their study to investigate the effect of magnesium supplement in lowering blood pressure of hypertensive diabetic patients, reported that during 4 month of supplementation with 450 mg/day elemental magnesium, serum magnesium concentration in the intervention group compared to placebo group, increased gradually and reached a significant level at the third month.[ 49 ] Regarding to this study and increment trend of serum magnesium in our study, this is possible that the duration of our study was inadequate to observe a significant difference in serum magnesium alterations. This resistance to change of serum magnesium levels could also be attributed to its important role as a cofactor and the need to precisely regulate its concentration. The results of this study show that as compared to the placebo group, in the experimental group dietary magnesium supplementation brought about statistically significant increase in serum renin concentration ( P  < 0.001). There is little information about sleep deficiency and HPA axis in scientific literature.[ 50 ] Simultaneous measurement of plasma renin level and changes in different sleep phases suggests a close relationship between renin, and REM and NREM sleep. NREM sleep occurred in association with increased plasma renin level, but decreased renin level is concurrent with lighter sleep. Spontaneous or stimulated awakening results in stopping the normal increase of the plasma renin. Therefore, plotting renin levels will show exactly the sleep phases. If the sleep cycles are normal, renin level fluctuates in regular periods, but in incomplete sleep cycles, the renin plot will reveal all structural sleep disorders.[ 51 ] The results of our study are consistent with the results obtained from the study of  Held et al . in which magnesium supplementation caused a significant increase in serum renin concentration in intervention group compared to placebo group. The proposed mechanism for this serum renin increment included sleep cycle alterations, and the endocrine glands which can affect the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activity through altering electrolytes level, including magnesium.[ 50 ] Some alterations occur in special regulatory pathways such as reduction of sensitivity to angiotensin II, due to sleep deficiency. Increased sleeping time, down-regulates inhibitory mechanism of renin release in kidney thus serum renin level increases. In adrenal cortex, it decrease aldosterone release and in hypothalamus, angiotensin II inhibits HPA axis.[ 52 ] The results of our study show that magnesium supplementation resulted in significant decrease in serum cortisol concentrations. The results of the present study are consistent with the results of Held study which showed that Mg 2+  supplementation caused significant cortisol reduction in the first half of the sleep.[ 31 ] However,  Cinar et al . reported that magnesium supplementation of 10 mg per kilogram of the body weight, for one month, if associated with physical activity could cause the increase in serum cortisol level in individuals.[ 53 ] One possible mechanism for this reducing effect is that the NMDA antagonist properties of magnesium, reduce the activity and secretion of adrenocorticotropin from anterior hypophysis through down-regulation of corticotropin releasing factor and its transportation via the main capillary network of hypophyseal port to anterior hypophysis. Which in turn, causes adenylyl cyclase activity in cell membrane of adrenal cortex, then reducing the activity of protein kinase A and decreasing conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone; the first and limiting reaction of cortisol synthesis. All mentioned actions are consistent with Mg 2+  antagonistic properties on NMDA. Beside NMDA antagonistic properties, Mg 2+  also has endocrine effects such as an ATII-antagonistic action[ 54 ] and a dampening effect on HPA-system activity[ 30 ] which results in decrease in serum cortisol concentration. The results of our study was not consistent with  Murck  and  Steiger  study, which in their study magnesium supplementation did not resulted in any decrement in serum cortisol concentrations. The solution they used in the treatment condition contained Mg 2+  as well as glucose. So the question arises, whether the effects could be due to this agent. Regarding the endocrine changes, ACTH is known to be increased by hypoglycemia. The secretion of the releasing peptide for ACTH, corticotropin-releasing hormone, in isolated rat hypothalamus is stimulated by glucose levels under 5.5 mM. Above this level, the changes are small and not significant. Thus, it seems unlikely that glucose might contribute to the observed effects but this cannot be completely ruled out. The results of our study showed that as compared to the placebo group, in the experimental group dietary magnesium supplementation brought about statistically significant increase in serum melatonin concentration ( P  = 0.007). Our result is consistent with the study of  Zhao et al . which suggested that magnesium sulfate injection to experimental rats caused the stimulation and significant increase of melatonin secretion from pineal gland.[ 51 ] Also the results of this study are consistent with the results of  Billyard's  study which stated that magnesium deficiency led to plasma melatonin reduction in rats. The induced magnesium deficiency was medium in this study which then increases its capability to extend the results to human (because severe magnesium deficiency is rare in human). However, since only plasma melatonin was measured in this study, it is not clear that the melatonin reduction was due to reduced synthesis or increased destruction of melatonin.[ 55 ] On the other hand, the results of  Murck  and  Steiger  study showed that no change was observed in cortisol, growth hormone, prolactin, and melatonin secretions due to magnesium supplementation.[ 30 ] In general, studies show that magnesium deficiency affects circadian cycle, melatonin reduction, and sleep disorders.[ 56 57 ] Morton and James suggested that the  N -acetyltransferase (NAT) activity in rat is increased after magnesium injection. Moreover, magnesium increases NAT activity in pineal gland  in vitro , suggesting that the pineal gland, not another place of the body, is the affect site.[ 58 ] The mentioned findings implicates on possible magnesium deficiency role in reduced NAT activity and reduced melatonin production. CONCLUSION Supplementation of magnesium appears to improve subjective and objective measures of insomnia in elderly people and may become a useful instrument in managing sleep disorders in the elderly, which could also be extended as a helpful aid to the general population.

Introduction Primary sleep disorders are those not associated with a medical condition, substance use or concurrent psychological disorder. In order to be diagnosed with a primary sleep disorder, the sleep disturbance must cause significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning  [1] . Nine percent of Americans report having insomnia  [2] . Thirty-five to forty percent of Americans report having problems falling asleep or excessive daytime sleepiness  [3] . Primary sleep disorders are often comorbid with psychiatric disorders, neurological and cardiovascular diseases  [4] . Average medical expenses of individuals with insomnia in the United States is nearly $2000 greater annual than those without sleep problems  [5] . Poor sleep is also associated with an increased risk of mortality, hospitalization and traffic accidents  [6] – [8] . First line treatment options for primary sleep disorders often include psychological or behavioral therapies  [9] . Sleep hygiene, sleep restriction, stimulus control, relaxation training and cognitive therapy are examples of such non-pharmacological therapies, all of which have shown some evidence of efficacy  [10] – [12] . Pharmacological treatments for primary sleep disorders, like insomnia, include benzodiazepine receptor agonists, benzodiazepines, sedating antidepressants and other drugs with sedating feature (anxiolytics, antipsychotics, antihistamines). Side-effects vary between these medications and can range from residual daytime sleepiness to dependence  [13] . There are many over-the-counter medications and herbal therapies that are used by individuals to treat insomnia. However the efficacy and side-effect profile of these substances are not as well known or studied as prescription medications  [14] . Many trials have been performed to assess the efficacy of exogenous melatonin in treating primary sleep disorders. Melatonin is a hormone secreted primarily by the pineal gland in response to variations in the circadian cycle and has been used for the last two decades for the treatment of sleep disorders in adults and children  [15] . In contrast to most available sleep medications, melatonin has little dependence potential, is not associated with habituation and typically produces no hangover. Given its reported hypnotic effects, relatively benign side-effect profile and over-the-counter availability, melatonin has been widely utilized in the United States  [16] . A previous meta-analysis demonstrated that melatonin was beneficial in treating most primary sleep disorders over the short-term (4 weeks or less)  [17] . However, since this meta-analysis, 7 trials have been published with an additional 1258 subjects. These additional trials nearly triple the sample size of previous meta-analyses. The additional power provided by these new trials will (1) allow us to more precisely estimate measures of treatment effects and (2) examine moderators of melatonin efficacy. Specifically, we will examine melatonin’s effects on sleep latency, total sleep time and sleep quality. We will also examine the moderating effects of measure type, dose and duration of melatonin treatment. Methods Selection of Studies PubMed was searched by two reviewers (AQ and EFO) using the terms “Melatonin” and “Sleep Disorder”. The search was further limited to include only randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses. The bibliographies of related reviews, meta-analyses and included articles were searched for additional eligible citations. All studies included were published before or on March 2012. Inclusion Criteria Trials were included if they (1) analyzed primary sleep disorders as defined by the DSM-IV, (2) examined the effects of melatonin, (3) were randomized placebo controlled trials, (4) had at least 10 participants for parallel designs or 5 participants for crossover designs and (5) were published in English. Disagreements regarding the inclusion of studies were discussed between the two reviewers (AQ and EFO) and ultimately decided by the third reviewer (MHB) when necessary. Meta-analytic Procedures Data was extracted using Microsoft Excel spreadsheets. Extracted data included sleep onset latency, total sleep time, sleep quality, age of sample, dose, duration, drug formulation. Sleep onset latency, total sleep time and sleep quality data were also classified in objective measures (polysomnography or actigraphy) and/or subjective (scales, questionnaires, sleep logs). Our primary outcome measure was mean improvement in sleep onset latency, total sleep time and sleep quality. In this meta-analysis, we considered sleep efficacy the same as sleep quality. We examined the difference between melatonin and placebo by calculating the weighted mean difference (WMD) using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (Biostat, Englewood, NJ) for sleep latency and total sleep time analysis. Sleep quality was analyzed in Comprehensive Meta-Analysis by calculating the standardized mean difference (SMD). SMD was favored over WMD for measuring sleep quality because rating scales assessing sleep quality differed between the included studies. A fixed-effects model was used for this meta-analysis with the results for a random-effects model presented as a sensitivity analysis. Publication bias was assessed by plotting the effect size against standard error for each trial (funnel plot)  [18] . In addition, publication bias was statistically tested by the Egger’s test and by determining the association between sample size and effect size in meta-regression  [18] . Heterogeneity between trials was determined by means of two separate statistical estimates using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis. First, a  Q- statistic was employed to provide a test of statistical significance indicating whether the differences in effect sizes are due to subject-level sampling error alone or other sources. In addition, we estimated heterogeneity using  I-square  statistic, which estimates the proportion of total variance that is attributable to between-study variance. For secondary analyses we performed several subgroup analyses and meta-regressions. Stratified subgroup analysis was used to assess the effects of type of measure (subjective/objective). We used the test for subgroup differences in Comprehensive Meta-Analysis to determine whether subgroups reduced overall heterogeneity  [19] . We initially intended to examine the effects of age group (children younger than 18 years old vs. adults older than 18 years old) on melatonin’s effects. However, there were not enough trials in children to conduct this analysis. Meta-regression was performed to examine the association between melatonin efficacy in trials and continuous variables such as (1) dose and (2) duration. Our threshold for statistical significance was selected to be p<.05 for the primary analysis, as well as for all subgroups analyses and meta-regression. Forest plots were generated separately on Microsoft Excel using previously published methods to aid in presentation of the results  [20] . All data including information on the inclusion/exclusion of studies and extraction of data for meta-analysis is available from the corresponding author by request. Results Included Studies We included nineteen studies involving a total of 1683 subjects in this meta-analysis  [21] – [39] . From the search on Pubmed and related bibliography above described 268 studies were selected. A total of 249 manuscripts were excluded for the following reasons: 123 were not randomized placebo controlled trials, 61 did not examine sleep disorders, 40 did not examine primary sleep disorders, thirteen did not examine the effects of melatonin, four did not have sample size fitting the inclusion criteria, five manuscripts were follow-up studies, two manuscripts were not in a peer-reviewed journal, and one study was retracted. Nineteen studies were included in the analysis, fourteen studies on the efficacy of melatonin for the treatment of insomnia, four studies on delayed sleep phase syndrome and one study on REM sleep behavior disorder.  Table 1  depicts the characteristics of included studies in this meta-analysis. 10.1371/journal.pone.0063773.t001 Table 1 Characteristics of Included Trials. Subjects randomly assigned to melatonin fell asleep 7 minutes earlier on average than subjects receiving placebo (weighted mean difference (WMD) = 7.06 minutes [95% CI: 4.37 to 9.75], Z = 5.15, p<0.001).  Figure 1  illustrates a forest plot depicting the estimated efficacy of melatonin from individual trials. There was significant evidence of heterogeneity between trials (Q = 31.9, df = 14, p = 0.004, I 2  = 56%). In the random effects model, sleep latency was reduced by over 10 minutes (WMD = 10.18 minutes [95% CI: 6.1 to 14.27], Z = 4.88, p<0.001). We found no significant evidence of publication bias based on the Egger’s Test (intercept = 1.08, [95% CI: −0.35 to 2.52], t = 1.62, p = 0.12). Stratifying trials by objective and subjective measures of sleep onset did not significantly reduce heterogeneity between trials (Q = 3, df = 1, p = 0.08). Melatonin significantly reduced sleep latency on both objective (WMD = 5.50 minutes [95% CI = 2.29 to 8.71], Z = 3.36, p<0.001) and subjective measures (WMD = 10.68 minutes [95% CI: 5.78 to 15.58], z = 4.27, p<0.001). Meta-regression demonstrated that trials of longer duration (parameter estimate (PE) = 0.53 [95% CI = 0.21 to 0.86], p = 0.001) reported greater effects on sleep latency. Trials using higher doses of melatonin also reported greater effects of melatonin on sleep latency at trend levels (PE = 1.95 [95% CI = −0.00 to 3.91], p = 0.05). 10.1371/journal.pone.0063773.g001 Figure 1 Efficacy of Melatonin in Reducing Sleep Latency. Subjects randomly assigned to melatonin had on average a total sleep time 8 minutes longer than subjects taking placebo (WMD = 8.25 minutes [95% CI: 1.74 to 14.75], Z = 2.48, p = 0.013). There was significant evidence of heterogeneity between trials (Q = 21.44, df = 12, p = 0.044, I 2  = 44%). Total sleep time was increased by 8 minutes in the random effects model (WMD = 8.48 minutes [95% CI: −4.02 to 20.98], Z = 1.33, p = 0.184). Subjects randomly assigned to melatonin had improvements in sleep quality compared to placebo (standardized mean difference (SMD) = 0.22 [95% CI: 0.12 to 0.32], Z = 4.52, p<0.001).  Figure 3  illustrates a forest plot depicting the estimated efficacy of melatonin from individual trials. No significant evidence of heterogeneity between trials was observed (Q = 11.59, df = 13, p = 0.56, I 2  = 0). A random effects model provided the same overall effect. We found no significant evidence of publication bias based on the Egger’s Test (intercept = −0.13 [95% CI: −1.08 to 0.81], t = 0.30, p = 0.76). Stratifying trials by objective and subjective measures of sleep quality did not reduce heterogeneity between trials (Q = 0.05, df = 1, p = 0.82). Melatonin improved sleep quality to a similar degree on both subjective (SMD = 0.23 [95% CI: 0.12 to 0.34], Z = 4.23, p<0.001) and objective measures (SMD = 0.20 [95% CI: −0.04 to 0.44], Z = 1.61, p = 0.10). Meta-regression demonstrated no significant effects of trial duration (PE = 0.005 [95% CI: −0.0006 to 0.012], p = 0.08) or dose of melatonin on sleep quality (PE = 0.011 [95% CI: −0.114 to 0.090], p = 0.81). 10.1371/journal.pone.0063773.g003 Figure 3 Effect of Melatonin on Sleep quality. SMD = standardized mean difference; CI = confidence interval. Discussion and Conclusion Our meta-analysis demonstrates that melatonin significantly improves sleep in subjects with primary sleep disorders compared to placebo. Melatonin reduces sleep-onset latency, increases total sleep time and improves overall sleep quality compared to placebo to a statistically significant degree. It should be noted that the improvements in sleep parameters in absolute terms were smaller than previous meta-analyses of benzodiazepines and newer non-benzodiazepine sleep medications. For instance, the reduction in sleep latency observed with melatonin in this meta-analysis, slightly less than 7 minutes, was less than sleep-latency reduction observed in previous meta-analyses of other available sleep medications. A previous meta-analysis demonstrated a significant benefit of benzodiazepines (10.0 to 19.6 minutes) and non-benzodiazepine sleep medicines (12.8 to 17 minutes) in reducing sleep-onset latency for primary sleep disorders  [21] . Thus prescription sleep medications are quite likely more effective than melatonin, although head-to-head trials could definitely alleviate any doubts regarding the relative efficacy of these agents. Meta-regressions were performed to assess the relationship between effect, duration and dose. Higher melatonin doses and longer duration trials were related to significant greater effect sizes on sleep latency and total sleep time. These findings suggest that there is no evidence of the development of tolerance with melatonin use. This stands in contrast to other commonly used hypnotics such as benzodiazepines  [13] . No greater effects in sleep quality were observed with melatonin dose or trial duration, suggesting that melatonin effects on sleep quality are constant for any duration or dose. Given our findings, it is important to note some limitations of this meta-analysis. Due to the relatively small number of trials that met our inclusion criteria, our meta-regression analysis had limited power. This problem was exacerbated by one trial that contributed a very large weight to our overall findings  [22] . The relatively small number of trials also limits the ability of the Egger’s Test to demonstrate publication bias. However there was no evidence of publication bias for all outcome measures on funnel plot as well. There were relatively few studies examining the efficacy of melatonin in children with primary sleep disorders and this precluded any stratified subgroup analysis based on age. The presence of mostly trials examining primary insomnia limited our ability to perform an analysis based on diagnoses. Despite these limitations, this meta-analysis demonstrated that exogenous melatonin administered to subjects with primary sleep disorders modestly improved sleep parameters including sleep latency, total sleep time and sleep quality. This finding corroborates the results of a previous meta-analysis conducted in the area several years ago that also demonstrated a significant benefit of melatonin  [17] . The benefits of melatonin compared to placebo appear smaller than that of available prescription sleep medications. However, melatonin should be considered in clinical practice due to its benign side-effect profile, cost and limited evidence of habituation and tolerance. Further research is needed to examine the long-term benefits of sleep medications including the comparative efficacy of melatonin to common prescription sleep medication.
